1.summary: Among the exiles by the river Chebar in Babylonia, Ezekiel sees a storm cloud open to reveal four living creatures, gleaming wheels and, above them, a throne bearing the likeness of Yahweh's glory.
1.lookfor: Notice how carefully Ezekiel piles up words like likeness and appearance, how the creatures and wheels move together without turning, and what he sees surrounding the figure on the throne.

names.name: Chebar
names.gloss: A river or irrigation canal in Babylonia where a community of Judean exiles had been settled.

names.name: Jehoiachin
names.gloss: King of Judah who surrendered to Nebuchadnezzar in 597 BC and was taken to Babylon with thousands of his people, Ezekiel among them.

names.name: Buzi
names.gloss: Ezekiel's father, known only from this verse.

names.name: Chaldeans
names.gloss: The people of southern Mesopotamia whose dynasty, including Nebuchadnezzar, ruled Babylon in this period.

insights.title: The thirtieth year
insights.body: Verse 2 dates the vision to the fifth year of Jehoiachin's exile, about 593 BC (1:2). The thirtieth year of verse 1 is unexplained, but a common view is that it was Ezekiel's age, the age at which priests began their service. If so, a priest who could never serve in the temple received his calling far from it.

insights.title: A canal near Nippur
insights.body: Babylonian documents from this era mention a large canal with a name matching Chebar near the city of Nippur. The Babylonians settled deported peoples in such farming districts to work the land. Ezekiel's community seems to have lived together, kept its elders and been free to gather in his house.

insights.title: Glowing metal
insights.body: The Hebrew word behind glowing metal (1:4, 1:27) is hashmal, which appears only in Ezekiel and whose exact meaning is uncertain. Ancient translators guessed at a shining alloy such as electrum. Modern Hebrew borrowed it as the word for electricity.

insights.title: The likeness of the appearance
insights.body: Ezekiel never says he saw God directly. He saw "the appearance of the likeness of Yahweh's glory" (1:28), layering qualifier on qualifier as if words keep failing him. The figure has the likeness of a man (1:26), yet the language holds the reader at a reverent distance.

insights.title: Four faces in Revelation
insights.body: The creatures' faces of man, lion, ox and eagle (1:10) reappear in Revelation's four living creatures around God's throne, there spread over four creatures. From the second century, Christian writers such as Irenaeus and Jerome linked the four faces with the four Gospels, though they matched them differently.

insights.title: God on wheels
insights.body: The throne moves on wheels that can go in any direction (1:17) and arrives in Babylonia, an unclean land far from the temple. For exiles who may have thought God was bound to Jerusalem, this was a startling message. Later chapters show the same glory leaving the temple and finally returning to a new one.

insights.title: The chariot in Jewish tradition
insights.body: Jewish tradition calls this vision the merkavah, the chariot, and treated it as so holy that the Mishnah restricts teaching it in public. It became the starting point of an early stream of Jewish mysticism. Ezekiel 1 is also the prophetic reading in synagogues on the festival of Shavuot.

insights.title: A rainbow round the throne
insights.body: The brightness around the figure on the throne looks like a rainbow in the clouds (1:28), recalling the sign God gave Noah after the flood. Why might a book that opens with judgment frame God's glory with a sign of his covenant promise?

2.summary: God calls Ezekiel "son of man" and sends him to a rebellious house, warning that they may not listen and giving him a scroll full of lament and woe.
2.lookfor: Count how often the people are called rebellious, notice what God says success will look like for Ezekiel, and watch what is written on the scroll.

insights.title: Son of man
insights.body: God addresses Ezekiel as ben adam, son of man (2:1), more than ninety times in the book, and never by his own name. In Hebrew the phrase simply means a human being, stressing how small and mortal the prophet is before the glory he has just seen. Daniel uses it for a heavenly figure, and Jesus takes it as his favourite way of speaking about himself.

insights.title: Exiles expecting a quick return
insights.body: Ezekiel's audience were the leading families taken in 597 BC, and many expected Babylon to fall and send them home soon. Jeremiah wrote to the same exiles telling them to settle in for seventy years. A message of further judgment on Jerusalem was not one they wanted to hear.

insights.title: Success without results
insights.body: God twice says the people may hear or refuse (2:5, 2:7), and promises only that "they will know that there has been a prophet among them" (2:5). Ezekiel's task is faithfulness, not persuasion. The same words return near the end of the judgment section, when events finally prove him right.

insights.title: Written on both sides
insights.body: Scrolls were normally written only on the inner side, so a scroll written "within and without" (2:10) was unusually full. The picture suggests a message already complete, with no space left to add anything. Its contents are lament, mourning and woe.

insights.title: The Spirit sets him up
insights.body: The Spirit enters Ezekiel and sets him on his feet (2:2), the first of many times the Spirit lifts or moves him. The book later promises that God will put his Spirit within the whole people. What happens to the prophet here becomes a sign of what God means to do for Israel.

insights.title: Briers and scorpions
insights.body: God tells Ezekiel not to fear though he lives among briers, thorns and scorpions (2:6), a picture of hostile listeners. Jeremiah received a similar charge not to be dismayed at his hearers' faces. Prophets were commonly warned of rejection before they began.

insights.title: Don't be rebellious
insights.body: Before giving Ezekiel the scroll, God warns him not to be rebellious like the people (2:8). Why might the messenger need the same warning as those he is sent to?

3.summary: Ezekiel eats the scroll, is made hard enough to face a hard people, sits stunned among the exiles at Tel Aviv for seven days, and is appointed a watchman before being shut in his house and made mute.
3.lookfor: Watch the taste of the scroll, the play on hardness, the duties of a watchman in verses 17 to 21, and the strange limits placed on Ezekiel's speech at the end.

names.name: Tel Aviv
names.gloss: The exiles' settlement by the Chebar; the name probably comes from a Babylonian phrase for an old ruin mound.

names.name: Chebar
names.gloss: The river or canal in Babylonia where the exiles lived.

insights.title: Sweet as honey
insights.body: The scroll of woe tastes "as sweet as honey" (3:3), yet Ezekiel then goes "in bitterness" (3:14). Jeremiah also speaks of eating God's words with joy. In Revelation, John eats a little scroll that is sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach, a clear echo of this scene.

insights.title: A play on Ezekiel's name
insights.body: Ezekiel's name, Yehezqel, means something like God strengthens or God makes hard. God says he has made Ezekiel's face hard and his forehead harder than flint (3:8-9), using the same root, hazaq. The people are hard-hearted (3:7), so their prophet is made harder still.

insights.title: Tel Aviv
insights.body: Tel Aviv (3:15) is probably a Hebrew form of a Babylonian name meaning a mound left by a flood, a word for an ancient ruin. In Hebrew it sounds like hill of spring. The modern Israeli city took its name from this verse by way of the Hebrew title of Theodor Herzl's novel Altneuland.

insights.title: Seven days overwhelmed
insights.body: Ezekiel sits among the exiles overwhelmed for seven days (3:15), the usual length of mourning. Job's friends sat silent beside him for seven days in the same way. Ezekiel absorbs what he has seen before he says a word.

insights.title: Blessed be Yahweh's glory
insights.body: "Blessed be Yahweh's glory from his place" (3:12) became part of the Kedushah, a central Jewish prayer, joined with the seraphim's song from Isaiah. The traditional Hebrew text reads blessed, though many scholars suggest a one-letter change giving the sound of the glory rising from its place.

insights.title: The watchman's charge
insights.body: A city watchman stood on the wall to warn of attack; if he stayed silent, the blood was on him (3:17-18). Ezekiel is made responsible for warning, not for the response. The charge is repeated almost word for word when Jerusalem falls.

insights.title: Bound and mute
insights.body: God says Ezekiel will be bound and his tongue stuck so he cannot rebuke the people, except when God opens his mouth (3:25-27). Since he goes on to speak many oracles, most interpreters take it as a ban on ordinary speech or on acting as the people's go-between. His mouth is fully opened only when news comes that Jerusalem has fallen.

insights.title: Blood on the watchman
insights.body: The watchman who keeps silent shares the blame for the death of the person he failed to warn (3:18). How does this weigh on anyone entrusted with speaking hard truths to others?

4.summary: Ezekiel acts out the siege of Jerusalem: he draws the city on a brick, lies on his side for months bearing the people's guilt, and eats rationed bread baked over dung.
4.lookfor: Notice each prop and posture Ezekiel uses, the numbers of days and what they stand for, and the moment the priest in him protests.

insights.title: A city on a brick
insights.body: The tile (4:1) was a sun-dried mud brick, the common writing and building material of Babylonia, where city plans were sometimes drawn on clay. Ezekiel builds a model siege with ramps and battering rams around it, the standard methods of Babylonian and Assyrian warfare. The iron pan between him and the city (4:3) may picture God's face set like a wall against Jerusalem.

insights.title: 390 and 40
insights.body: Ezekiel lies 390 days on his left side for Israel and 40 on his right for Judah (4:5-6). No explanation of the 390 has won agreement: some count roughly from the building of Solomon's temple or the division of the kingdom to the exile. The ancient Greek translation reads 190, and the total of 430 matches the years Israel spent in Egypt.

insights.title: A day for a year
insights.body: "Each day for a year" (4:6) recalls the forty years of wandering, one year for each day the spies explored Canaan. The principle later became a tool for some Christian interpreters who calculated prophetic timelines, though Ezekiel uses it only as a sign. Here the prophet bears the years in his own body.

insights.title: Siege rations
insights.body: Twenty shekels of bread is often estimated at around eight ounces, a little over 200 grams, and a sixth of a hin of water at roughly half a litre a day (4:10-11). The mixed grains suggest scraping together whatever is left. In the real siege the bread ran out completely.

insights.title: A priest's protest
insights.body: Ezekiel is told to bake his bread over human dung (4:12), and he objects that he has never eaten anything unclean (4:14). As a priest he was bound by strict food laws. God allows cow dung instead, a common fuel in the region, but the point stands: exiles will eat unclean food among the nations (4:13).

insights.title: Bearing their iniquity
insights.body: Ezekiel is to "bear their iniquity" (4:4-5), using the Hebrew phrase nasa awon. In priestly law the phrase can mean either suffering punishment for sin or carrying it away, as the scapegoat did. Christian readers have often heard an echo of it in the servant who bears the sins of many in Isaiah.

insights.title: Prophecy acted out
insights.body: Ezekiel performs more symbolic actions than any other prophet. Isaiah walked barefoot and Jeremiah wore a yoke, but Ezekiel's signs go on for months and involve his whole body. In ancient thought such acts did not just illustrate the message; they set it in motion.

5.summary: Ezekiel shaves his head and beard with a sword and divides the hair into thirds to show the fate of Jerusalem's people, then God explains that the city at the centre of the nations has sinned worse than the nations.
5.lookfor: Follow each third of the hair, notice the few strands tucked into his robe and what happens to some of them, and watch the list of judgments at the end.

insights.title: A razor for a priest
insights.body: Priests were forbidden to shave their heads or the corners of their beards, so shaving with a sword (5:1) was a shocking act for Ezekiel. Forced shaving was a mark of humiliation, as when David's envoys were sent home half-shaved. Isaiah had used the same image of a hired razor for Assyria.

insights.title: Even the remnant burned
insights.body: Ezekiel binds a few hairs in his robe (5:3), a picture of a protected remnant. Then some of those are thrown in the fire too (5:4). Even survivors are not safe simply because they survived; the theme of a small, purified remnant returns later.

insights.title: In the middle of the nations
insights.body: God says he set Jerusalem "in the middle of the nations" (5:5), as a showcase of his ways. Later Jewish and Christian tradition spoke of Jerusalem as the navel of the earth, and medieval maps placed it at the centre. Here the privileged position makes her failure worse, since she rebelled more than the nations around her (5:6).

insights.title: The curses of the covenant
insights.body: Parents eating children (5:10), sword, famine, pestilence and wild animals (5:17) come straight from the covenant curses in Leviticus and Deuteronomy. Lamentations records that such horrors happened in the siege. Ezekiel presents the fall of Jerusalem as the covenant's warnings coming true.

insights.title: They will know
insights.body: "They will know that I, Yahweh, have spoken" (5:13) is a form of the book's signature refrain, which appears in some form roughly seventy times. Its point is that events, not arguments, will finally make God known. The phrase is used for Israel and the nations, in judgment and in restoration.

insights.title: Defiling the sanctuary
insights.body: The reason given for the harshest judgment is that the people defiled God's sanctuary with detestable things (5:11). For a priest like Ezekiel, the temple's holiness was the centre of everything. Chapters 8 to 11 will show what that defilement looked like.

insights.title: I will be comforted
insights.body: God says his wrath will come to rest and "I will be comforted" (5:13), a startlingly human way to speak of him. How do you understand the Bible's language of divine anger alongside its descriptions of God's patience and pity?

6.summary: Ezekiel prophesies against the mountains of Israel, where the high places stand, announcing that idols and altars will be smashed among the bodies of their worshippers, while a remnant will remember God in exile.
6.lookfor: Notice who and what is addressed, the repeated phrase about knowing Yahweh, and the change of tone in verses 8 to 10 about those who escape.

names.name: Diblah
names.gloss: An unknown place, possibly a copying error for Riblah in Syria, marking the far northern edge of the land.

insights.title: Why the mountains
insights.body: The high places were hilltop shrines where Israelites worshipped Yahweh, other gods or both, often with altars and incense stands. Kings Hezekiah and Josiah tried to close them, but they kept coming back. So God addresses the mountains themselves (6:3).

insights.title: Dung-idols
insights.body: Ezekiel's favourite word for idols is gillulim, which he uses far more than any other book. Many scholars think it was coined from a root linked to dung, giving a scornful sense like dung-gods. The word appears here in nearly every verse (6:4-6, 6:9, 6:13).

insights.title: Bones around the altars
insights.body: Scattering bones around altars (6:5) made them permanently unclean. Josiah did exactly this at the altar of Bethel, fulfilling an old prophecy. Ezekiel turns the worshippers themselves into the defilement of their shrines.

insights.title: God's broken heart
insights.body: In exile the remnant will remember "how I have been broken with their lewd heart" (6:9). The Hebrew is difficult and translations differ, but many read it as God himself wounded by their unfaithfulness. Ezekiel pictures idolatry as adultery, an image he develops at length in chapters 16 and 23.

insights.title: Under every green tree
insights.body: Every high hill, every green tree and every thick oak (6:13) is the standard language of Canaanite-style hilltop worship. Deuteronomy commands such sites to be destroyed. The phrase works like a catalogue of everywhere Israel had looked for blessing apart from the temple.

insights.title: Mountains condemned, mountains blessed
insights.body: Chapter 6 speaks against the mountains of Israel. Chapter 36 speaks to the same mountains with a promise that they will be replanted and repopulated. The book's structure moves from judgment to restoration on the same ground.

insights.title: Loathing and remembering
insights.body: The survivors will loathe themselves when they remember what they did (6:9). Is self-loathing here an end in itself, or a step toward knowing God?

7.summary: In short, breathless poems Ezekiel announces that the end has come on the whole land: a day of wrath in which wealth is useless, defences fail and every kind of leader is helpless.
7.lookfor: Listen for the repeated words end, day and comes, notice what happens to buying, selling, silver and gold, and watch how each group of leaders is left without answers.

insights.title: The end has come
insights.body: "The end has come" (7:2, 7:6) echoes Amos a century and a half earlier, who saw a basket of summer fruit and heard that the end had come on Israel. Amos spoke to the northern kingdom; Ezekiel applies the same verdict to the whole land.

insights.title: The day of Yahweh
insights.body: The day (7:7, 7:10) is the day of Yahweh, a theme of the prophets in which God acts decisively in judgment. Zephaniah, shortly before Ezekiel, also said that silver and gold could not rescue anyone on that day. The New Testament carries the idea forward as the day of the Lord.

insights.title: Buyer and seller
insights.body: Israelite law allowed sold land to return to its family at the Jubilee or to be bought back by a relative. Ezekiel says the buyer should not rejoice nor the seller mourn (7:12), because no one will be left to hold or reclaim anything. The normal rhythm of property and inheritance is suspended.

insights.title: The rod has blossomed
insights.body: "The rod has blossomed. Pride has budded" (7:10). The image is open: the rod may be Babylon, God's instrument, or Judah's own arrogance and violence (7:11). Some readers hear an ironic echo of Aaron's staff that budded as a sign of God's choice.

insights.title: His secret place
insights.body: God says strangers will profane "my secret place" (7:22). The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning to hide or treasure, and most take it as the temple, perhaps its innermost room. Its beauty, given for God's majesty, had been used for idols (7:20).

insights.title: No vision, law or counsel
insights.body: People will seek a vision from the prophet, but the law will perish from the priest and counsel from the elders (7:26). Jeremiah's enemies had boasted that law, counsel and prophecy could never fail them. Every source of guidance Judah relied on would go silent at once.

insights.title: Silver in the streets
insights.body: People will throw their silver into the streets because it cannot save them (7:19). What do people trust in that would prove just as useless on such a day?

8.summary: Lifted by the hair in a vision, Ezekiel is taken to the Jerusalem temple and shown four scenes of abomination, each worse than the last, being practised in God's own house.
8.lookfor: Track each of the four scenes and where in the temple it happens, who is involved, and what the worshippers say about Yahweh.

names.name: Jaazaniah
names.gloss: A leading elder burning incense to images; his family had once been known for supporting reform.

names.name: Shaphan
names.gloss: Probably King Josiah's secretary, who read the newly found book of the law to the king.

names.name: Tammuz
names.gloss: A Mesopotamian god, Dumuzi in Sumerian, whose death was ritually mourned each year.

insights.title: September 592 BC
insights.body: The date (8:1) works out to about September 592 BC, a year and two months after Ezekiel's call. The elders of Judah are sitting in his house in Babylonia when the vision comes. He is carried to Jerusalem "in the visions of God" (8:3), not bodily.

insights.title: The image of jealousy
insights.body: The word for image, semel, is rare and is used of the idol King Manasseh set in the temple. Many think the image of jealousy (8:3) was a restored version of it, perhaps an image of the goddess Asherah. It provokes Yahweh to jealousy because it puts a rival in his house.

insights.title: The son of Shaphan
insights.body: Jaazaniah son of Shaphan leads the secret incense rite (8:11). Shaphan's family had backed Josiah's reform, and his son Ahikam protected Jeremiah. Even a reforming family has a member burning incense to painted animals.

insights.title: Weeping for Tammuz
insights.body: Tammuz (8:14) was the Mesopotamian shepherd god Dumuzi, whose descent to the underworld was mourned in summer rites. The Babylonian month named after him survives as Tammuz in the Jewish calendar. Women weeping for a foreign god at the temple gate shows how deeply Babylonian religion had reached Jerusalem.

insights.title: Backs to the temple
insights.body: About twenty-five men stand between porch and altar, the area reserved for priests, with their backs to the temple, bowing to the sun (8:16). Josiah had removed the horses dedicated to the sun from the temple entrance. Turning one's back on God's house was a picture of apostasy itself.

insights.title: The branch to their nose
insights.body: "They put the branch to their nose" (8:17) is one of the most obscure lines in the book. It may describe a ritual gesture known from ancient Near Eastern worship. An old Jewish tradition holds that scribes softened an original reading, "to my nose," meaning an insult thrown in God's face.

insights.title: Yahweh doesn't see us
insights.body: The elders in the dark say, "Yahweh doesn't see us. Yahweh has forsaken the land" (8:12). They have concluded that God has left, so they look elsewhere. The irony is that he does see, and the next chapters show his glory really leaving, because of what they are doing.

insights.title: Rooms of imagery
insights.body: The elders practise their idolatry hidden "in the dark, every man in his rooms of imagery" (8:12). What might the private rooms of imagery look like in a life that is outwardly devout?

9.summary: In the vision, a man in linen marks the foreheads of those who grieve over Jerusalem's abominations, while six executioners strike down everyone else, beginning at the temple.
9.lookfor: Watch who receives the mark and why, where the slaughter begins, how Ezekiel responds, and where God's glory is standing as it happens.

insights.title: The mark of tav
insights.body: The mark on the foreheads (9:4) is in Hebrew a tav, the last letter of the alphabet, which in the old script was written as an X or a cross. Early Christian writers such as Tertullian saw in it a foreshadowing of the cross. In Ezekiel it simply identifies those God protects.

insights.title: Sealed on their foreheads
insights.body: Revelation pictures God's servants sealed on their foreheads before judgment falls, and its locusts may harm only those without the seal. Both scenes recall the blood on the doorposts at the first Passover, which marked the households the destroyer passed over.

insights.title: Those who sigh and cry
insights.body: The mark goes not to the outwardly religious but to those who "sigh and that cry over all the abominations" (9:4). What saves them is grief over the city's sin, not innocence of it. Scripture elsewhere describes righteous Lot as distressed by what he saw in Sodom.

insights.title: Begin at my sanctuary
insights.body: Judgment begins at the sanctuary, with the elders standing before the house (9:6). First Peter says that judgment begins with the household of God. Those closest to holy things bear the greatest responsibility.

insights.title: The man in linen
insights.body: Linen was the dress of priests, especially the high priest on the Day of Atonement, and in Daniel a heavenly messenger is also clothed in linen. The man here carries a scribe's writing kit (9:2), a case for reed pens and ink worn at the belt. He records and marks; the six others carry weapons.

insights.title: A vision of the coming slaughter
insights.body: The killing of old and young alike (9:6) is terrible to read. In the vision it portrays, as God's verdict, the destruction the Babylonian army would bring on Jerusalem a few years later. Ezekiel himself falls on his face and pleads for what is left of Israel (9:8), as Abraham pleaded for Sodom.

insights.title: Glory on the threshold
insights.body: Before the killing starts, the glory moves from the cherub to the threshold of the temple (9:3). It is the first stage of a slow departure across chapters 9 to 11. God does not leave all at once.

insights.title: Yahweh doesn't see
insights.body: The people justify themselves by saying God has forsaken the land and does not see (9:9). How might a belief that God is absent or indifferent shape the way people live?

10.summary: Coals from between the cherubim are scattered over the city, and Ezekiel watches the cherubim and wheels, which he now recognises as the creatures he saw by the Chebar, carry Yahweh's glory to the temple's east gate.
10.lookfor: Compare this description with chapter 1, notice what is different about the faces, and follow the glory's movement step by step.

names.name: Chebar
names.gloss: The river or canal in Babylonia where Ezekiel first saw the living creatures.

insights.title: The cloud leaves
insights.body: When Solomon dedicated the temple, the cloud filled the house and the priests could not stand to minister. Here the cloud fills the house again (10:4), but this time as the glory prepares to leave. The scene runs the dedication in reverse.

insights.title: Enthroned on the cherubim
insights.body: Israel's psalms call Yahweh the one who sits above the cherubim, and two great carved cherubim spread their wings over the ark in Solomon's temple. Ezekiel now realises that the creatures of his first vision are cherubim (10:20). The throne he saw in Babylonia is the same throne as the temple's.

insights.title: Where did the ox go?
insights.body: In chapter 1 each creature had the faces of a man, a lion, an ox and an eagle; here the ox is replaced by "the face of the cherub" (10:14). One explanation is that a cherub's face was thought of as bull-like, like the great winged bull statues that guarded Mesopotamian palaces. Others suspect a difference in the text's transmission.

insights.title: Coals that burn, not cleanse
insights.body: In Isaiah's call a seraph takes a coal from the altar and touches the prophet's lips to cleanse him. Here coals from among the cherubim are scattered over the city (10:2) to burn it. The same holy fire purifies or destroys.

insights.title: The whirling wheels
insights.body: The wheels are called "the whirling wheels" (10:13), Hebrew galgal, a word linked with rolling and with whirlwinds. Jewish tradition later made the ofanim and galgalim, wheels, into orders of angels in its prayers. Here the wheels are full of eyes, suggesting that nothing escapes God's sight (10:12).

insights.title: Guardians of holy places
insights.body: Across the ancient Near East, composite winged beings guarded thrones, temples and palaces. Israel's cherubim belonged to this world, guarding Eden and the inner sanctuary. In Ezekiel they are not static statues but the living bearers of God's mobile throne.

insights.title: Leaving by the east gate
insights.body: The glory pauses at the east gate (10:19), the main entrance facing the sunrise. What does it suggest that God's departure is gradual, as if reluctant, rather than sudden?

11.summary: Ezekiel prophesies against Jerusalem's leaders who think they are safe as meat in a cauldron, one of them drops dead, and God promises the exiles a sanctuary in exile, a new heart and a return, before his glory leaves the city.
11.lookfor: Notice the leaders' proverb and how God turns it around, what happens to Pelatiah, who claims the land, and where the glory stops when it leaves.

names.name: Jaazaniah
names.gloss: A leader at the east gate, son of Azzur; not the same man as the Jaazaniah of chapter 8.

names.name: Pelatiah
names.gloss: One of Jerusalem's princes, whose sudden death shakes Ezekiel; his name means roughly Yahweh rescues.

names.name: Chaldea
names.gloss: Babylonia, where Ezekiel and the exiles lived.

insights.title: The cauldron and the meat
insights.body: "This is the cauldron, and we are the meat" (11:3) means: we who stayed in Jerusalem are the choice cuts, protected by the city's walls. God answers that the only meat left in the pot will be the bodies of those they killed (11:7). The image returns in a darker form in chapter 24.

insights.title: Who owns the future?
insights.body: Those left in Jerusalem told the exiles, "Go far away from Yahweh. This land has been given to us" (11:15). They assumed the deported had been rejected by God. God reverses this: the future lies with the exiles, a point Jeremiah also made with his vision of good and bad figs.

insights.title: A little sanctuary
insights.body: God says he will be to the exiles "a sanctuary for a little while" (11:16). The Hebrew miqdash me'at can also mean a small sanctuary. The Talmud applies the phrase to synagogues and houses of study, the places where Jews met God without a temple.

insights.title: A heart of flesh
insights.body: God promises to remove the stony heart and give a heart of flesh and a new spirit (11:19). Ezekiel repeats the promise more fully later, and Jeremiah speaks of the law written on the heart. Paul draws on this language for the work of the Spirit on human hearts.

insights.title: Pelatiah dies
insights.body: As Ezekiel prophesies, Pelatiah drops dead (11:13), and Ezekiel cries out that God is making a full end of the remnant. Whether this happened in Jerusalem at that moment or belongs within the vision is debated. Either way, the prophet's first reaction is anguish, not triumph.

insights.title: The glory on the Mount of Olives
insights.body: The glory leaves the city and stops on the mountain to the east (11:23), the Mount of Olives. Zechariah later pictures God's feet standing there on the day of the Lord. A rabbinic tradition says the divine presence lingered on that mountain, waiting for the people to repent.

insights.title: Present in exile
insights.body: The exiles had lost temple, land and king, yet God promises to be their sanctuary where they are (11:16). What changes when people discover that God can be found far from the places they associated with him?

12.summary: Ezekiel packs an exile's bag, digs through a wall at dusk and leaves with his face covered, acting out the coming flight and capture of Jerusalem's prince, and then rebuts sayings that prophetic warnings never come true.
12.lookfor: Follow each step of the sign and the details God adds about the prince, then notice the two popular sayings at the end and how God answers them.

names.name: Chaldeans
names.gloss: The Babylonians, whose land the prince will be taken to.

insights.title: Fulfilled in Zedekiah
insights.body: The prince who digs through the wall at night and is taken in a net (12:12-13) is Zedekiah, Judah's last king. Second Kings and Jeremiah record that he fled at night through a gap in the wall, was caught near Jericho, saw his sons killed, was blinded and was taken to Babylon. That explains the riddle that he would die in Babylon without seeing it (12:13).

insights.title: Prince, not king
insights.body: Ezekiel calls Zedekiah nasi, prince (12:10), not king. He seems to regard the exiled Jehoiachin as the legitimate king, which is why he dates events by Jehoiachin's exile. The word nasi later becomes his title for the ruler of the restored people.

insights.title: An exile's bundle
insights.body: Assyrian palace reliefs show deportees carrying small bundles on their shoulders as they are marched away. Ezekiel's sack is "stuff for moving" (12:3), the little that exiles could carry. Digging through a mud-brick wall (12:5) was possible by hand.

insights.title: Eyes that don't see
insights.body: The people "have eyes to see, and don't see" (12:2), echoing Jeremiah and Isaiah. Jesus uses the same words when his disciples fail to understand. Ezekiel's signs are meant to provoke the question "What are you doing?" (12:9).

insights.title: Every vision fails
insights.body: A popular saying claimed that time passes and every prophetic vision comes to nothing (12:22). Another said Ezekiel's visions were for the distant future (12:27). God answers that his word will no longer be delayed. Jerusalem fell about six years after this.

insights.title: Survivors as witnesses
insights.body: God leaves a few alive so that they can tell the nations of their own abominations (12:16). The survivors become evidence that the judgment was deserved. The theme returns in chapter 14.

insights.title: Eating with trembling
insights.body: Ezekiel eats and drinks with trembling as a sign (12:18). What might it mean to live with that kind of seriousness about what is coming, without being paralysed by fear?

13.summary: Ezekiel denounces prophets who invent messages of peace and whitewash a crumbling wall, and women who use charms and veils to control people's lives for payment.
13.lookfor: Look for the images of foxes, gaps and whitewash, the repeated word peace, and the strange equipment of the women in verses 17 to 23.

insights.title: Peace when there is no peace
insights.body: The false prophets say "Peace" when there is none (13:10, 13:16). Jeremiah used almost the same words against prophets in Jerusalem, and the two prophets were confronting the same message at the same time. Hananiah's promise of a quick return is a known example.

insights.title: Whitewash on a weak wall
insights.body: A flimsy wall of loose stones could be made to look solid with a coat of plaster or whitewash (13:10). The first heavy rain would bring it down. Jesus calls hypocrites whitewashed tombs, and Paul calls a high priest a whitewashed wall.

insights.title: Foxes and gaps
insights.body: The prophets are like foxes in ruins (13:4), scavengers making their home in the rubble rather than repairing it. They have not gone up into the gaps (13:5). Later God says he looked for someone to stand in the gap and found no one.

insights.title: Out of their own heart
insights.body: The false prophets speak "out of their own heart" (13:2) and follow their own spirit (13:3). The test of a prophet in Israel was whether God had sent them and whether their word came true. Ezekiel's own messages come from outside him, often against his will.

insights.title: Bands and veils
insights.body: The women sew bands on wrists and make head coverings to "hunt souls" (13:18). The exact practice is uncertain, but many scholars compare Babylonian magic, which used knotted bands and cloths for binding and releasing spells. They are paid in barley and bread (13:19). The Bible also honours true women prophets such as Huldah; the charge here is divination, not that women prophesied.

insights.title: Written in the register
insights.body: False prophets will not be written in the writing of the house of Israel (13:9), probably the citizen list of those who would return. Ezra later records families excluded because they could not find their names. The image grows into the book of life in later Scripture.

insights.title: Grieving the righteous
insights.body: The false prophets grieve the righteous and encourage the wicked (13:22). How can comforting words do harm, and how can one tell real comfort from false reassurance?

14.summary: Elders who cherish idols in their hearts come to consult Ezekiel and are told God will answer them himself, and God declares that even Noah, Daniel and Job could save only themselves from a land under judgment.
14.lookfor: Notice where the idols are located in verse 3, the hard statement about deceived prophets, and the repeated example of three righteous men.

names.name: Daniel
names.gloss: A proverbially righteous man; possibly the Daniel of the book of Daniel, or an ancient hero of the same name.

insights.title: Idols in the heart
insights.body: These elders have "taken their idols into their heart" (14:3). They may have no statue at home, but their loyalties are divided. God refuses to be consulted as one oracle among several.

insights.title: Which Daniel?
insights.body: The Hebrew spelling here, Dan'el, differs slightly from the Daniel of the book of Daniel. Many scholars link him with Danel, a righteous king known from ancient Ugaritic poems, which fits his pairing with Noah and Job as ancient non-Israelite figures. Others, including much Jewish and Christian tradition, identify him with Ezekiel's younger contemporary in Babylon.

insights.title: Righteousness that saves only oneself
insights.body: Abraham once asked if Sodom might be spared for a few righteous people. Ezekiel says that in Jerusalem's case even the most famous righteous men would save only themselves, not their children (14:16). Jeremiah says the same of Moses and Samuel.

insights.title: God deceiving a prophet
insights.body: "I, Yahweh, have deceived that prophet" (14:9) is a hard saying. It echoes the story of Micaiah, where God allows a lying spirit to entice prophets who were already telling a king what he wanted. Most interpreters read it as God giving people over to the deception they have chosen, while both prophet and inquirer still bear guilt (14:10).

insights.title: Four severe judgments
insights.body: Sword, famine, evil animals and pestilence (14:21) are a standard set of covenant curses. Revelation gives the rider on the pale horse power to kill by the same four. In Ezekiel they mark judgment as total.

insights.title: A strange comfort
insights.body: Survivors from Jerusalem will come to the exiles, and seeing their conduct will "comfort" them (14:22-23). The comfort is that the exiles will understand God did not act without cause. The point is not pleasure in suffering but the vindication of God's justice.

insights.title: Faith passed on?
insights.body: Not even Noah, Daniel or Job could save their sons and daughters by their own righteousness (14:20). What does this suggest about the limits of inherited faith?

15.summary: In a short parable, Jerusalem is compared to the wood of a vine, useless for building even before it is burned and worse than useless after it has been through the fire.
15.lookfor: Notice that the parable is about the wood, not the fruit, and pay attention to which parts have already been burned.

insights.title: Good for nothing but fuel
insights.body: Vine wood is twisted, soft and thin, too weak to make even a peg for hanging a pot (15:3). Its only value is its fruit; once pruned or dead, it is fuel. Ezekiel's question is pointed: what is a vine good for if it bears no fruit?

insights.title: Israel the vine
insights.body: Israel was often pictured as God's vine or vineyard, a source of national pride. Isaiah's song of the vineyard and Psalm 80 use the image, and Jeremiah calls Israel a choice vine turned wild. Ezekiel deliberately removes any grounds for pride in it.

insights.title: Branches thrown into the fire
insights.body: Jesus calls himself the true vine and says that branches that do not remain in him are thrown into the fire and burned. The image draws on this chapter and the other vine passages. For Ezekiel and for Jesus, a vine's value lies entirely in its fruitfulness.

insights.title: Burned at both ends
insights.body: The fire has already burned both ends and charred the middle (15:4). Many see this as Judah after the invasions and the deportation of 597 BC: what remains in Jerusalem is the scorched middle. If the wood was useless whole, it is less use now (15:5).

insights.title: A trespass
insights.body: The land is made desolate because "they have committed a trespass" (15:8). The Hebrew word ma'al means a breach of faith, especially the misuse of what belongs to God. It is used of Judah's final unfaithfulness in Chronicles.

insights.title: From the fire into the fire
insights.body: Those who escape one fire will be consumed by another (15:7). For the people of Jerusalem, surviving 597 BC had seemed proof of God's favour. Ezekiel tells them it was only a reprieve.

insights.title: What is it good for?
insights.body: The parable judges the vine purely by its usefulness for fruit. What does this short chapter suggest about the purpose of being chosen?

16.summary: In a long and shocking allegory, God tells Jerusalem's story as that of an abandoned baby girl he rescued, raised and married, who became a faithless wife; judgment follows, but the chapter ends with a promise of an everlasting covenant.
16.lookfor: Trace the stages of the story from birth to marriage to betrayal, notice the sisters Samaria and Sodom, and watch how the ending differs from what the rest of the chapter leads you to expect.

names.name: Amorite
names.gloss: One of the peoples of Canaan before Israel; here a figure for Jerusalem's pagan ancestry.

names.name: Hittite
names.gloss: A people of Anatolia and Syria, and a name for some of Canaan's earlier inhabitants.

names.name: Samaria
names.gloss: Capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, destroyed by Assyria in 722 BC.

names.name: Sodom
names.gloss: The city destroyed in Abraham's day, a byword for wickedness.

names.name: Philistines
names.gloss: Israel's neighbours and old enemies on the southern coast.

names.name: Chaldea
names.gloss: Babylonia, called here the land of merchants.

insights.title: A newborn's care
insights.body: Cutting the cord, washing, rubbing with salt and wrapping in cloth (16:4) were normal care for a newborn; rubbing with salt was thought to firm and cleanse the skin. Leaving unwanted infants exposed in the open was known in the ancient world. Jerusalem is pictured as a baby no one wanted.

insights.title: An Amorite and a Hittite
insights.body: Jerusalem was a Canaanite city long before David captured it from the Jebusites. Saying her father was an Amorite and her mother a Hittite (16:3) strips her of any claim to a holy pedigree. Whatever she became was God's gift, not her birthright.

insights.title: Though you are in your blood, live
insights.body: "Though you are in your blood, live!" (16:6) is recited at the Jewish circumcision ceremony, and verses from this passage appear in the Passover Haggadah's telling of Israel's growth in Egypt. A line from an indictment became a blessing over every newborn son.

insights.title: Spreading the skirt
insights.body: God says, "I spread my skirt over you" (16:8), a gesture of taking a woman under one's protection in marriage. Ruth asks Boaz to do the same. The covenant at Sinai is here pictured as a wedding.

insights.title: A disturbing metaphor
insights.body: The prophets often pictured Israel as God's wife and idolatry as adultery, but Ezekiel's version is unusually graphic, including the stripping and violent punishment of the woman (16:37-41). It was aimed to shock a male, elite audience into seeing their own betrayal. Many modern readers, including many scholars, find it deeply troubling, and the Mishnah records a view that this chapter should not be read publicly as a prophetic reading.

insights.title: Children through the fire
insights.body: The worst charge is that she sacrificed the children she bore to God (16:20-21). Child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom is condemned by Jeremiah and was ended by Josiah. Ezekiel calls them "my children" (16:21).

insights.title: The sin of Sodom
insights.body: Ezekiel names Sodom's iniquity as pride, plenty, ease and neglect of the poor and needy, together with abomination (16:49-50). Genesis and the letter of Jude emphasise its sexual violence and immorality. Interpreters weigh these passages differently, but Ezekiel's list is a reminder that comfort and indifference were part of the charge.

insights.title: An everlasting covenant
insights.body: After all the judgment, God promises to remember his covenant and establish an everlasting one (16:60), even restoring Samaria and Sodom (16:53). The people will be silenced by shame not when punished but "when I have forgiven you" (16:63). Grace, not judgment, has the last word.

17.summary: Ezekiel tells a riddle of two eagles, a cedar and a vine to expose King Zedekiah's broken oath to Babylon, and ends with God himself planting a tender cedar shoot on Israel's high mountain.
17.lookfor: Try to decode the riddle before reading the explanation in verses 11 to 21, then compare the first eagle's planting with God's planting at the end.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: The mountains north of Israel famous for cedars; here a figure for the royal house in Jerusalem.

names.name: Pharaoh
names.gloss: The king of Egypt, probably Hophra (Apries), whose help Zedekiah sought against Babylon.

insights.title: A riddle and a parable
insights.body: God tells Ezekiel to "tell a riddle, and speak a parable" (17:2). The Hebrew words are hidah, a puzzle to be solved, as with Samson's riddle, and mashal, a comparison or proverb. The riddle is told first and solved afterwards (17:12), drawing the hearers in before the verdict.

insights.title: Decoding the eagles
insights.body: The first great eagle is Nebuchadnezzar, who took the top of the cedar, King Jehoiachin, to Babylon, the city of merchants (17:4, 17:12). The seed he planted is Zedekiah, made a vassal king. The second eagle is Pharaoh, to whom Zedekiah turned for horses and troops (17:15).

insights.title: A vassal's oath
insights.body: Ancient treaties bound a lesser king to his overlord by oaths sworn before the gods, with curses for breaking them. Chronicles says Nebuchadnezzar made Zedekiah swear by God. That is why God calls it "my oath" and "my covenant" (17:19): breaking it was a sin against Yahweh, not just bad politics.

insights.title: The cedar of Lebanon
insights.body: Jerusalem's palace was panelled with cedar from Lebanon, and Solomon built a great hall called the House of the Forest of Lebanon. Jeremiah addresses the royal house as one who nests in the cedars. The cedar top is the Davidic dynasty.

insights.title: A tender shoot
insights.body: At the end God takes a tender twig from the cedar and plants it on a high mountain, where it becomes a great tree (17:22-23). This is a promise of a future king from David's line. Isaiah and Jeremiah use similar images of a shoot and a branch, which Christians have read as fulfilled in Jesus.

insights.title: Birds in its branches
insights.body: Birds of every kind will dwell in the cedar's shade (17:23), a picture of nations finding shelter under God's king. Daniel uses the image for Nebuchadnezzar's kingdom, and Jesus echoes it in his parable of the mustard seed that becomes a tree.

insights.title: Bringing down the high tree
insights.body: God says he brings down the high tree and exalts the low, dries the green and makes the dry flourish (17:24). Where else in Scripture does God reverse human expectations in this way, and what does it say about him?

18.summary: God rejects the proverb that children suffer for their parents' sins, declaring that each person lives or dies by his own way, that anyone can turn, and that he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked.
18.lookfor: Notice the three generations in the case study, the specific behaviours listed for the righteous man, and the closing call to turn and live.

insights.title: Sour grapes
insights.body: The exiles' proverb, "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge" (18:2), blamed their suffering on past generations. Jeremiah quotes it too. It bred fatalism: if we are paying for our parents' sins, nothing we do can change things.

insights.title: Each for his own sin
insights.body: Ezekiel insists that the son will not bear the father's iniquity (18:20). Deuteronomy already forbade courts to execute children for their parents' crimes, while the Ten Commandments speak of consequences reaching later generations. Scholars debate whether Ezekiel is introducing a new individualism or, more likely, freeing his own generation from a sense of inherited doom.

insights.title: A portrait of the righteous
insights.body: The righteous man (18:5-9) avoids hilltop idol feasts, adultery and contact during menstruation, returns pledges, does not rob, feeds the hungry, clothes the naked, and lends without interest. Psalms 15 and 24 contain similar checklists for who may enter God's presence. Worship, sexual ethics and economic justice belong together.

insights.title: The returned pledge
insights.body: A creditor could take a poor man's cloak as a pledge but had to return it by sunset, since he slept in it. Ezekiel lists returning the pledge (18:7) alongside avoiding idolatry. Small acts of economic mercy are counted as righteousness.

insights.title: Not equal
insights.body: The people complain that the Lord's way "is not equal" (18:25). The Hebrew verb, takan, means to weigh or measure, so the charge is that God's scales are rigged. God turns it back: it is their measuring that is crooked.

insights.title: No pleasure in death
insights.body: "Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked?" (18:23), and "Turn yourselves, and live!" (18:32) are among the clearest statements of God's will to save in the Old Testament. The New Testament speaks of God desiring all people to be saved and not wishing any to perish.

insights.title: Make yourself a new heart
insights.body: Here God commands, "make yourself a new heart and a new spirit" (18:31), but in chapter 36 he promises to give one. How do you hold together human responsibility to turn and God's gift of a changed heart?

19.summary: Ezekiel sings a funeral lament for Judah's princes, picturing their mother as a lioness whose cubs are captured and as a fruitful vine now burned and replanted in the desert.
19.lookfor: Notice the two cubs and where each is taken, then the change of image to a vine, and the last line describing the poem itself.

insights.title: A funeral song
insights.body: The chapter is a qinah, a lament (19:1, 19:14), a funeral song usually written in a limping rhythm of a longer line followed by a shorter one. David's lament for Saul and Jonathan and the book of Lamentations use the same form. Here it is sung for a dynasty that is still alive, as if already dead.

insights.title: Who are the cubs?
insights.body: The first cub, taken to Egypt with hooks (19:4), is clearly Jehoahaz, deposed by Pharaoh Neco in 609 BC. The second, taken to Babylon in a cage (19:9), is either Jehoiachin or Zedekiah; interpreters are divided. The lioness may be Judah itself or Hamutal, the mother of both Jehoahaz and Zedekiah.

insights.title: The lion of Judah
insights.body: Jacob's blessing calls Judah a lion's cub and promises that the sceptre will not depart from him. Ezekiel's lament plays on that old image: the lioness and her royal cubs end up in pits and cages. Revelation later names Christ the Lion of the tribe of Judah.

insights.title: Hooks and cages
insights.body: Assyrian reliefs show lions being hunted with nets and kept in cages for royal hunts. The same reliefs and inscriptions describe captive kings led by hooks or rings and displayed in cages. Chronicles says Manasseh was taken to Babylon with hooks.

insights.title: Fire from its own branches
insights.body: The vine once had strong branches fit for sceptres (19:11), but fire goes out from one of its own branches and devours it (19:14). The destruction starts from within the royal line. Most see a reference to Zedekiah, whose rebellion brought the Babylonian army.

insights.title: No sceptre left
insights.body: The poem ends with no strong branch left to rule (19:14). Yet in chapter 17 God had promised to plant a tender shoot, and in chapter 21 the crown waits for the one whose right it is. Ezekiel laments the end of the kings he knew without abandoning the promise to David.

insights.title: Mourning before the end
insights.body: "This is a lamentation, and shall be for a lamentation" (19:14): it is sung before the final fall and will still be sung after. What might it mean to grieve something before it is fully lost?

20.summary: When elders come to consult him, God retells Israel's history as rebellion after rebellion, from Egypt to the present, stayed only by his concern for his name, then promises a new exodus that will purge the rebels and bring the people home.
20.lookfor: Track the repeated pattern of gift, rebellion, threatened wrath and restraint for my name's sake, and watch for the surprising claims in verses 25 and 32.

names.name: Bamah
names.gloss: Hebrew for a high place or hilltop shrine, used here in a scornful pun.

insights.title: August 591 BC
insights.body: The date (20:1) is about August 591 BC, eleven months after the vision of chapter 8. Again the elders come to inquire, and again God refuses to be consulted by them (20:3, 20:31). Instead of an oracle about the future, they get a history lesson.

insights.title: Idols in Egypt
insights.body: Ezekiel says Israel worshipped Egypt's idols even before the exodus (20:7-8), something the book of Exodus does not narrate. Joshua also tells Israel to put away the gods their fathers served in Egypt. Ezekiel's retelling is bleaker than any other in Scripture: there was never a golden age.

insights.title: For my name's sake
insights.body: Four times God restrains his anger "for my name's sake" (20:9, 20:14, 20:22, 20:44). In the ancient world a god's name stood for his reputation among the nations. Israel's survival rests not on its merit but on God's commitment to his own character.

insights.title: He will live in them
insights.body: God's statutes are those "which if a man does, he will live in them" (20:11), quoting Leviticus. Paul cites the same words twice in his discussion of law and faith. In Ezekiel the point is that the law was a gift of life that Israel refused.

insights.title: Statutes that were not good
insights.body: "I gave them statutes that were not good" (20:25) is one of the hardest lines in the book. Many interpreters read it as God handing the people over to the corrupt practices they chose, including child sacrifice (20:26), much as Paul speaks of God giving people up. Others think it refers to a distorted reading of the law about the firstborn.

insights.title: Passing under the rod
insights.body: "I will cause you to pass under the rod" (20:37) pictures a shepherd counting sheep one by one as they pass under his staff, setting some apart. Leviticus uses the same image for tithing the flock. In the new exodus God will sort his people individually (20:38).

insights.title: Like the nations
insights.body: Some exiles were saying, "We will be as the nations" (20:32), ready to blend into Babylon and worship wood and stone. God refuses to let his people disappear: "I will be king over you" (20:33). The threat of assimilation in exile was real, and this chapter answers it.

insights.title: A speaker of parables
insights.body: The chapter ends with Ezekiel complaining that people dismiss him as a speaker of parables (20:49). In Hebrew Bibles this short oracle begins chapter 21, so verse numbers differ from here to the end of the next chapter. How can vivid images become a way for listeners to avoid the message?

21.summary: God draws his sword against Jerusalem in a fierce song, Ezekiel pictures Nebuchadnezzar choosing by divination between Jerusalem and Ammon's capital, the crown is taken from Judah's prince, and Ammon too is sentenced.
21.lookfor: Listen to the sword song's repetitions, follow the king of Babylon at the fork in the road, and notice the promise hidden in verse 27.

names.name: Rabbah
names.gloss: Capital of the Ammonites, the site of modern Amman in Jordan.

names.name: Ammon
names.gloss: A people east of the Jordan, Judah's neighbours and sometime allies against Babylon.

insights.title: Three ways to ask the gods
insights.body: At the fork in the road the king of Babylon shakes arrows, consults teraphim, and looks in the liver (21:21). Drawing marked arrows, consulting household images, and reading the livers of sacrificed sheep were all known methods of divination; archaeologists have found clay liver models used to train Babylonian diviners. God steers even pagan omens to his purpose.

insights.title: Jerusalem or Rabbah
insights.body: Judah and Ammon had both rebelled against Babylon, and Nebuchadnezzar had to decide which to attack first. The lot falls on Jerusalem (21:22). Ammon is not spared for long (21:28), and later an Ammonite king backed the murder of Babylon's governor in Judah.

insights.title: Drawn and not returned
insights.body: Earlier prophets had spoken of God's sword, but here it is sharpened, polished and swung again and again (21:9-17). The sword "will not return any more" (21:5) to its sheath. Ezekiel is to sigh with a broken heart before the people (21:6), so that they ask why.

insights.title: Remove the turban
insights.body: "Remove the turban, and take off the crown" (21:26). The word for turban, mitsnefet, is used elsewhere of the high priest's headdress, so some see both priestly and royal leadership ending. The triple "overturn" (21:27) in Hebrew is a single word repeated, a crashing emphasis.

insights.title: Until he comes whose right it is
insights.body: The crown will be no more "until he comes whose right it is" (21:27). This closely echoes Jacob's blessing of Judah, that the sceptre would not depart until he comes to whom it belongs. Jewish and Christian interpreters alike have read both verses as pointing to a coming king.

insights.title: Exalt the low
insights.body: "Exalt that which is low, and humble that which is high" (21:26) is a refrain of biblical reversal. Hannah sings it and Mary echoes it in her song. Here it announces the fall of Judah's proud prince.

insights.title: Judgment for the neighbours too
insights.body: The last oracle turns to Ammon (21:28-32), who will be remembered no more. It anticipates the oracles against the nations in chapters 25 to 32, beginning with Ammon. God's judgment begins with his own people but does not stop there.

insights.title: The sigh as a sermon
insights.body: Ezekiel's broken-hearted sighing is itself the message (21:6-7). When can grief speak more powerfully than argument?

22.summary: Ezekiel indicts Jerusalem as the bloody city, lists its crimes against family, neighbour and God, pictures it as dross melted in a furnace, and finds no one among its leaders to stand in the gap.
22.lookfor: Notice how many times the words in you and blood recur, how every class of leader is named in verses 25 to 29, and what God looks for in verse 30.

insights.title: The holiness code broken
insights.body: The crimes listed in verses 6 to 12, from dishonouring parents to incest, bribes and interest, track closely with the laws of Leviticus 18 to 20. Ezekiel shows the city breaking the very code that defined Israel as holy. The charge ends, "and have forgotten me" (22:12).

insights.title: The bloody city
insights.body: Ezekiel calls Jerusalem "the bloody city" (22:2), literally city of bloods, the Hebrew plural for bloodshed or bloodguilt. Nahum used the same phrase of Nineveh. Jerusalem has become like the empire it once feared.

insights.title: Silver and dross
insights.body: Silver ore was refined by melting it with lead in a furnace; the lead absorbed impurities and left dross behind. God says the whole people have become dross (22:18), with no silver left. Isaiah and Jeremiah use the same image, and Malachi pictures God as a refiner purifying silver.

insights.title: A roll call of failure
insights.body: Prophets, priests, princes and the people of the land all fail (22:25-29). Zephaniah, writing a generation earlier, used strikingly similar language about lions, wolves and priests who do violence to the law. Ezekiel seems to build on his predecessor.

insights.title: Holy and common
insights.body: The priests have made no distinction between the holy and the common or the clean and unclean (22:26). Teaching that distinction was a core priestly duty from the beginning. In Ezekiel's restored temple the priests will teach it again.

insights.title: No one in the gap
insights.body: "I sought for a man among them who would build up the wall and stand in the gap... but I found no one" (22:30). Moses had once stood in the breach to turn away God's wrath. The verse has been widely used of intercession, and Christian readers have heard in it the need that Christ fills.

insights.title: The foreigner, widow and orphan
insights.body: Among the city's sins are oppressing the foreigner and wronging the fatherless and widow (22:7, 22:29). Why do the prophets so often measure a society's faithfulness by how it treats those with least power?

23.summary: In a second, even more graphic allegory, Samaria and Jerusalem are pictured as two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, whose political alliances with Assyria, Babylon and Egypt are treated as adultery and end in their destruction.
23.lookfor: Notice which foreign powers each sister turns to, the cup Jerusalem is given to drink, and the charges about the sanctuary in verses 38 and 39.

names.name: Oholah
names.gloss: The elder sister, standing for Samaria; the name means something like her tent.

names.name: Oholibah
names.gloss: The younger sister, standing for Jerusalem; the name means something like my tent is in her.

names.name: Pekod
names.gloss: An Aramean tribe east of the Tigris, part of Babylon's empire.

names.name: Shoa
names.gloss: A people in Babylon's empire, probably from east of the Tigris.

names.name: Koa
names.gloss: Another eastern people allied with Babylon; often paired with Shoa.

insights.title: Two tents
insights.body: Oholah probably means her tent and Oholibah my tent is in her (23:4). Tent is the word used for the tabernacle. Many think the names contrast Samaria's own shrines with Jerusalem, where God's own sanctuary stood, which makes her betrayal worse.

insights.title: Alliances as adultery
insights.body: Unlike chapter 16, the focus here is on foreign policy. Samaria turned to Assyria, paying tribute and later rebelling, and Jerusalem courted Babylon and then Egypt (23:5, 23:16, 23:19). Seeking security from empires meant taking on their gods and trusting them instead of Yahweh.

insights.title: Painted in red
insights.body: Oholibah falls for images of Chaldeans "portrayed with red" (23:14) on walls. Babylonian and Assyrian palaces were decorated with painted and glazed images of officials and soldiers. The Assyrians' blue uniforms and horsemen (23:6) are the glamour of imperial power.

insights.title: Nose and ears
insights.body: "They will take away your nose and your ears" (23:25) reflects real punishments: some ancient Near Eastern law codes prescribed cutting off the nose of an adulteress, and Assyrian kings boasted of mutilating captives. Like chapter 16, the chapter's violence against a female figure is deeply disturbing, and many readers today handle it with great care.

insights.title: Your sister's cup
insights.body: Jerusalem will drink her sister's cup, deep and wide, full of horror and desolation (23:32-33). The cup of God's wrath is a recurring prophetic image, and Jesus speaks of the cup he must drink in Gethsemane.

insights.title: The same day
insights.body: The sisters killed their children for idols and then on the same day came into God's sanctuary (23:38-39). For Ezekiel the mixing is the horror: atrocity and worship side by side, as if nothing had happened. Jeremiah condemned the same pattern in his temple sermon.

insights.title: Samaria's fate as warning
insights.body: Oholah's destruction by Assyria (23:9-10) happened in 722 BC, more than a century before Ezekiel. Jerusalem saw it and did worse (23:11). Kings draws the same lesson, and Jeremiah says faithless Israel looks righteous compared with treacherous Judah.

insights.title: Seeking safety elsewhere
insights.body: The sisters looked to powerful nations for security rather than to God. What modern forms might that same temptation take, for nations or churches?

24.summary: On the day Babylon's siege of Jerusalem begins, Ezekiel tells a parable of a rusted cooking pot, and that evening his wife dies; forbidden to mourn, he becomes a sign of the grief too deep for mourning that is coming.
24.lookfor: Notice the exact date and what Ezekiel is told to do with it, how the cooking pot parable changes from chapter 11, and the details of mourning Ezekiel must not perform.

insights.title: Write the name of the day
insights.body: The date (24:1) is the day Nebuchadnezzar's siege of Jerusalem began, usually placed in January 588 BC; Kings gives the same day. Ezekiel is told to write it down (24:2), so that when news arrives no one can say he guessed afterwards. Jewish tradition still keeps the fast of the Tenth of Tevet on this date.

insights.title: The pot revisited
insights.body: In chapter 11 Jerusalem's leaders boasted that the city was the cauldron and they were the meat. Now the pot is put on the fire, the meat boiled until the bones burn, and the empty pot heated to burn off its rust (24:10-11). Their saying is turned into their sentence.

insights.title: Blood on the bare rock
insights.body: The law required that the blood of a slaughtered animal be poured out and covered with dust. Jerusalem has left blood on the bare rock, uncovered (24:7). Like Abel's blood crying from the ground, uncovered blood was thought to call for justice.

insights.title: The desire of your eyes
insights.body: Ezekiel's wife, "the desire of your eyes" (24:16), dies suddenly in the evening (24:18). It is one of very few personal details in the book, told in a single sentence. The same phrase is then used of the temple, the desire of the people's eyes (24:21).

insights.title: Forbidden to mourn
insights.body: Mourners normally removed their headdress, went barefoot, covered the lower face and ate bread brought by neighbours. Ezekiel must do none of these (24:17). The sign is that the coming loss of temple and children will be too overwhelming for the usual rituals (24:22-23).

insights.title: Ezekiel will be a sign
insights.body: "Thus Ezekiel will be a sign to you" (24:24) is only the second time the prophet's name appears in the book, after the opening verses. The word for sign, mofet, often means a portent or wonder. Ezekiel's own bereavement becomes God's message.

insights.title: Waiting for the messenger
insights.body: God tells Ezekiel that a survivor will come with the news, and then his mouth will be opened (24:26-27). The book now turns to the nations for eight chapters while the siege runs its course. The fugitive arrives in chapter 33.

insights.title: Obedience in grief
insights.body: Ezekiel did as he was commanded the morning after his wife died (24:18). What do you make of a calling that reached even into the prophet's private grief?

25.summary: Ezekiel turns to Judah's neighbours, pronouncing judgment on Ammon, Moab, Edom and the Philistines for gloating over and taking revenge on Judah in its downfall.
25.lookfor: Notice the pattern of because and therefore in each short oracle, and what each nation said or did when Judah fell.

names.name: Ammon
names.gloss: A people east of the Jordan, with its capital at Rabbah.

names.name: Rabbah
names.gloss: Capital of Ammon, today's Amman in Jordan.

names.name: Moab
names.gloss: A people east of the Dead Sea, descended in Genesis from Lot.

names.name: Seir
names.gloss: The mountain country of Edom, south-east of the Dead Sea.

names.name: Edom
names.gloss: Descendants of Esau, Jacob's brother, living south-east of Judah.

names.name: Teman
names.gloss: A region or town of Edom.

names.name: Dedan
names.gloss: An oasis trading centre in north-west Arabia.

names.name: Cherethites
names.gloss: A coastal people linked with the Philistines, probably from Crete; some served as David's bodyguard.

insights.title: Seven nations in the gap
insights.body: Chapters 25 to 32 hold oracles against seven nations: Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia, Tyre, Sidon and Egypt. They sit between the start of the siege (chapter 24) and the news of Jerusalem's fall (chapter 33). Babylon, God's instrument in this period, is not among them.

insights.title: Aha!
insights.body: Ammon's crime is saying "Aha!" over the profaned sanctuary and clapping and stamping with contempt (25:3, 25:6). Gloating over a neighbour's ruin is treated as a serious offence. Obadiah condemns Edom in the same terms.

insights.title: Edom's revenge
insights.body: Edom took vengeance on Judah (25:12), apparently helping Babylon and seizing territory in the south. Psalm 137 remembers the Edomites shouting, Raze it, on the day Jerusalem fell. The bitterness between the brother nations of Jacob and Esau runs through the Bible.

insights.title: The children of the east
insights.body: Ammon and Moab are handed to "the children of the east" (25:4, 25:10), the desert tribes beyond the Jordan. Within a few centuries both kingdoms had faded as Arab peoples, including the Nabataeans, moved into their lands. Rabbah becoming a pasture for camels (25:5) pictures that takeover.

insights.title: Like all the nations
insights.body: Moab and Seir say Judah "is like all the nations" (25:8). The claim denies that Israel had any special relationship with God. It is the same thing some of the exiles wished were true.

insights.title: Philistines from Crete
insights.body: The Cherethites (25:16) were probably Cretans, and the Philistines are said to have come from Caphtor, usually identified with Crete. They arrived on the coast of Canaan as part of the movements of the Sea Peoples around 1200 BC. Babylon destroyed their cities in the decades before Ezekiel.

insights.title: The sin of gloating
insights.body: None of these nations caused Jerusalem's fall, yet each is judged for how it reacted. Why might the Bible treat rejoicing at someone else's disaster so seriously?

26.summary: Because Tyre rejoiced at Jerusalem's fall as a chance for profit, God announces that many nations, led by Nebuchadnezzar, will reduce the island city to a bare rock, and the sea peoples will lament its fall.
26.lookfor: Notice why Tyre is happy about Jerusalem, the image of the bare rock and drying nets, and how the princes of the sea respond.

names.name: Tyre
names.gloss: A wealthy Phoenician port on an island just off the coast of Lebanon, the trading hub of the eastern Mediterranean.

names.name: Nebuchadnezzar
names.gloss: King of Babylon (605 to 562 BC), who destroyed Jerusalem and besieged Tyre.

insights.title: The gateway of the peoples
insights.body: Tyre rejoices that Jerusalem, "the gateway of the peoples" (26:2), is broken, because trade will flow to Tyre instead. Jerusalem sat on inland trade routes that competed with Tyre's networks. The city sees a neighbour's catastrophe as a business opportunity.

insights.title: The rock made bare
insights.body: In Hebrew Tyre is Tsor, meaning rock. God says he will make her "a bare rock" (26:4, 26:14), a place to spread fishing nets. The proud island fortress will be reduced to what its name says it is.

insights.title: Thirteen years of siege
insights.body: According to the Jewish historian Josephus, drawing on Phoenician records, Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for thirteen years. The island city seems to have submitted without being destroyed, and Ezekiel himself later notes that Babylon gained no wages from it. The prophecy shifts from "many nations" (26:3) to Nebuchadnezzar (26:7) and back to "they" (26:12).

insights.title: Stones in the water
insights.body: "They will lay your stones, your timber, and your dust in the middle of the waters" (26:12). In 332 BC Alexander the Great captured the island by building a causeway from the rubble of the mainland city, and many interpreters see this verse fulfilled there. Others read the chapter's language as the poetic imagery of total destruction.

insights.title: The kings and merchants mourn
insights.body: The princes of the sea step down from their thrones and lament (26:16-17). Revelation's lament over Babylon the great borrows heavily from Ezekiel's oracles on Tyre, with kings, merchants and sailors standing far off and weeping. Tyre becomes a type of every proud commercial power.

insights.title: Down to the pit
insights.body: God will bring Tyre down to the pit, to the people of old time (26:20). The pit is Sheol, the realm of the dead, pictured as a place beneath the earth. The theme of nations going down to the pit returns in the oracles on Egypt.

insights.title: Profit from others' ruin
insights.body: Tyre's sin is to calculate its gain from Jerusalem's loss (26:2). Where might people today be tempted to see others' disasters chiefly as opportunities?

27.summary: Ezekiel sings a lament over Tyre pictured as a magnificent merchant ship, built from the finest materials and crewed and supplied by nations far and wide, which sinks in the heart of the seas.
27.lookfor: Enjoy the ship's construction in verses 4 to 11, skim the long list of trading partners, and watch what happens to the ship and how the sailors react.

names.name: Senir
names.gloss: The Amorite name for Mount Hermon, north of Israel, a source of timber.

names.name: Bashan
names.gloss: A fertile region east of the Sea of Galilee, known for oaks and cattle.

names.name: Kittim
names.gloss: Cyprus, named after its city Kition, and later a name for western coastlands.

names.name: Elishah
names.gloss: Probably Cyprus or part of it, known from other ancient sources as Alashiya.

names.name: Arvad
names.gloss: A Phoenician island city north of Tyre.

names.name: Gebal
names.gloss: The Phoenician port of Byblos, famous for skilled shipwrights.

names.name: Tarshish
names.gloss: A distant western source of metals, often linked with Tartessos in Spain.

names.name: Javan
names.gloss: The Ionian Greeks of the Aegean and Asia Minor.

skim.advice: Verses 12 to 24 are a catalogue of Tyre's trading partners and goods; skim the place names, but notice what Judah and Israel supplied and the trade in human beings.

insights.title: Perfect in beauty
insights.body: Tyre says, "I am perfect in beauty" (27:3). The same phrase was used of Zion, and Lamentations records passers-by mocking Jerusalem as the city once called the perfection of beauty. Tyre has claimed a title that belonged to God's city.

insights.title: A ship of the whole world
insights.body: Tyre the ship has planks from Hermon, a cedar mast from Lebanon, oak oars from Bashan, linen sails from Egypt and dyed awnings from Cyprus (27:5-7). Phoenicians were the great seafarers of their age, founding colonies such as Carthage. The poem is one of the richest ancient descriptions of Mediterranean trade.

insights.title: Blue and purple
insights.body: Blue and purple cloth (27:7, 27:16) were luxury goods, dyed with a costly extract of murex sea snails in which the Phoenicians specialised. The very name Phoenician may come from a Greek word for the purple-red colour. The same dyes were used for the tabernacle's curtains.

insights.title: Selling people
insights.body: Javan, Tubal and Meshech "traded the persons of men" (27:13), that is, slaves. Joel accuses Tyre and Sidon of selling the people of Judah to the Greeks. Revelation's list of Babylon's cargo ends with "people's bodies and souls."

insights.title: Wheat from Judah
insights.body: Judah and Israel supplied wheat, honey, oil and balm (27:17). Since Solomon's day, Israel had traded farm produce for Phoenician timber and skill. Ezekiel's own people were part of the economy he is lamenting.

insights.title: Broken by the east wind
insights.body: "The east wind has broken you in the heart of the seas" (27:26). A psalm praises God for breaking the ships of Tarshish with the east wind. In Revelation, sailors watching Babylon burn cry out, much as these mariners do (27:29-32).

insights.title: A lament for an enemy
insights.body: Ezekiel is told to take up a lamentation over Tyre (27:2), as he did for Judah's princes. The poem is full of admiration for what is being lost. Judgment on the nations in the prophets is not always triumphant; it can be mournful.

insights.title: Who is like Tyre?
insights.body: The sailors cry, "Who is there like Tyre?" (27:32). What does the chapter suggest about building identity and security on wealth and global trade?

28.summary: God rebukes the ruler of Tyre who claims to be a god, laments his fall in language of Eden and a guardian cherub, condemns Sidon, and promises that Israel will one day live securely in its land.
28.lookfor: Notice the ruler's claim in verse 2, the images of Eden, precious stones and a cherub in verses 12 to 19, and the turn to Israel's future at the end.

names.name: Daniel
names.gloss: A proverbially wise and righteous figure, as in chapter 14.

names.name: Eden
names.gloss: The garden of God in Genesis 2 to 3.

names.name: Sidon
names.gloss: A Phoenician port north of Tyre, its older sister city.

insights.title: I am a god
insights.body: The ruler of Tyre says, "I am a god, I sit in the seat of God" (28:2). Ancient kings often claimed divine status or descent. The refrain answers him twice: "you are man, and not God" (28:2, 28:9). King Herod's death in Acts follows a similar pattern.

insights.title: Precious stones
insights.body: The nine stones that adorn the king (28:13) match nine of the twelve on the high priest's breastpiece. The ancient Greek translation lists all twelve. The king of Tyre is pictured almost as a priest in God's garden.

insights.title: A fallen cherub?
insights.body: The anointed cherub cast out of God's mountain for pride (28:14-17) has been read since early Christian writers such as Origen and Tertullian, often alongside Isaiah 14, as describing the fall of Satan. Most modern interpreters, and Jewish tradition, read it as a poetic portrait of the king of Tyre, drawing on stories of Eden and the first human. Both readings see pride as the root of the fall.

insights.title: Wisdom and wealth
insights.body: Tyre's wealth came from shrewd trade (28:4-5), and Phoenicians were famous for skill in navigation, crafts and commerce. Hiram of Tyre had helped Solomon build the temple. Ezekiel concedes the wisdom but condemns the violence and pride it bred (28:16-17).

insights.title: The death of the uncircumcised
insights.body: "You will die the death of the uncircumcised" (28:10) means a shameful death with no honourable burial. For an Israelite audience it was the most dishonourable end imaginable. The phrase prepares for the underworld scene of chapter 32.

insights.title: Israel secure
