insights.body: At the centre of the oracles against the nations comes a promise: Israel will be gathered and live securely, building houses and planting vineyards (28:25-26). Once the scornful neighbours are dealt with, God's people will have peace. It is a preview of chapters 34 to 37.

insights.title: Tyre and Sidon in the Gospels
insights.body: Jesus later says Tyre and Sidon would have repented if they had seen his miracles, and he heals a Syrophoenician woman's daughter in their region. The cities judged here become places where God's mercy reaches Gentiles.

insights.title: Corrupted wisdom
insights.body: "You have corrupted your wisdom by reason of your splendor" (28:17). How can gifts like beauty, intelligence or success become the very things that lead someone astray?

29.summary: God condemns Pharaoh as a great river monster who claims to have made the Nile, promises to humble Egypt for forty years, and in a much later oracle gives Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as wages for his unpaid siege of Tyre.
29.lookfor: Notice Pharaoh's boast, the image of Egypt as a reed staff, and the very different date of the oracle in verses 17 to 21.

names.name: Pharaoh
names.gloss: The king of Egypt, here probably Hophra (Apries), who ruled about 589 to 570 BC.

names.name: Seveneh
names.gloss: Syene, modern Aswan, on Egypt's southern frontier.

names.name: Ethiopia
names.gloss: Cush, the Nile kingdom south of Egypt, in today's Sudan.

names.name: Pathros
names.gloss: Upper (southern) Egypt, regarded as the Egyptians' homeland.

names.name: Nebuchadnezzar
names.gloss: King of Babylon, God's instrument against Judah, Tyre and Egypt.

insights.title: The great monster
insights.body: Pharaoh is "the great monster that lies in the middle of his rivers" (29:3). The Hebrew tannin can mean a sea serpent or dragon, and here it evokes the Nile crocodile. Other passages use the same word for the chaos monster that God defeats.

insights.title: My river is my own
insights.body: Pharaoh says, "My river is my own, and I have made it for myself" (29:3). Egypt's life depended entirely on the Nile, and the king was its guarantor. Claiming to have made the river is claiming the Creator's place.

insights.title: A staff of reed
insights.body: Egypt has been "a staff of reed" to Israel (29:6), snapping and wounding whoever leans on it. An Assyrian officer had mocked Hezekiah with the same image a century before. Judah kept trusting Egypt, and Zedekiah's hope in Pharaoh's army had just failed.

insights.title: From Syene to Cush
insights.body: "From the tower of Seveneh even to the border of Ethiopia" (29:10) means the whole length of Egypt, like Dan to Beersheba for Israel. Syene, at Aswan, sat near the island of Elephantine, where a Jewish military colony lived in the following century.

insights.title: Forty years
insights.body: Egypt will be desolate for forty years and then restored as a lowly kingdom (29:11-14). No surviving record shows a forty-year desolation of Egypt; Babylon invaded about 568 BC, but Egypt stayed independent until the Persians took it in 525 BC. Many read the forty years as a symbolic generation, like Israel's wilderness years.

insights.title: No wages from Tyre
insights.body: Dated to about 571 BC, verses 17 to 21 are the latest oracle in the book. God says Nebuchadnezzar's army laboured against Tyre until heads were rubbed bald, but got no wages, so Egypt will be his payment (29:18-19). The book openly preserves an earlier prophecy alongside this update, a sign of how its first readers understood prophecy and fulfilment.

insights.title: A horn will sprout
insights.body: God will "cause a horn to sprout for the house of Israel" (29:21). A horn is a symbol of strength, and in the Psalms a sprouting horn is linked to David's line. Zechariah's song in Luke uses the same language of a horn of salvation.

30.summary: A lament proclaims the day of Yahweh on Egypt and its allies, naming Egypt's great cities one by one, and God says he has broken Pharaoh's arm and will strengthen the arm of Babylon's king.
30.lookfor: Listen for the day of Yahweh language, skim the roll of Egyptian cities, and watch the contrast between the two kings' arms.

names.name: Put
names.gloss: A people of North Africa, probably Libya, who served Egypt as soldiers.

names.name: Lud
names.gloss: A people, possibly the Lydians of Asia Minor, known as mercenaries.

names.name: Memphis
names.gloss: Ancient capital of Lower Egypt, near modern Cairo.

names.name: Zoan
names.gloss: Tanis, a royal city in the Nile delta.

names.name: No
names.gloss: Thebes, the great city of Upper Egypt, modern Luxor.

names.name: Sin
names.gloss: Pelusium, Egypt's fortress on its north-eastern border.

names.name: Aven
names.gloss: On, or Heliopolis, centre of sun worship; the Hebrew spelling also means wickedness.

names.name: Tehaphnehes
names.gloss: Tahpanhes, a border fortress where Jeremiah was taken after Jerusalem fell.

skim.advice: Verses 13 to 18 list Egypt's cities in turn; skim the names, but notice that judgment reaches every part of the land and its gods.

insights.title: The day of Yahweh for Egypt
insights.body: "The day is near, even Yahweh's day is near" (30:3). The prophets had turned the day of Yahweh, once expected as Israel's victory, into a day of judgment on Israel itself. Here it falls on the nations too.

insights.title: Egypt's mercenaries
insights.body: Ethiopia, Put, Lud and "all the mixed people" (30:5) were Egypt's allies and hired troops. Pharaohs of this period relied heavily on foreign soldiers, including Greeks and Carians, as well as Libyans and Nubians. When Egypt falls, so do those who depend on it (30:6).

insights.title: Every city named
insights.body: Memphis, Pathros, Zoan, Thebes, Pelusium, Heliopolis, Bubastis and Tahpanhes (30:13-18) span Egypt from the delta to the far south. Naming each city makes the judgment concrete. The idols of Memphis are singled out (30:13), recalling the plagues as judgment on Egypt's gods.

insights.title: Tahpanhes
insights.body: Tahpanhes (30:18) is where the Judeans who fled to Egypt after Jerusalem fell, taking Jeremiah with them, settled. Jeremiah buried stones at the entrance to Pharaoh's house there as a sign that Nebuchadnezzar would come. Ezekiel and Jeremiah agree that Egypt was no refuge.

insights.title: The broken arm
insights.body: The oracle about Pharaoh's broken arm is dated to about April 587 BC (30:20-21), soon after an Egyptian army marched to relieve besieged Jerusalem and then withdrew. Jeremiah had predicted the retreat. Judah's last hope of outside rescue had failed.

insights.title: Two arms
insights.body: Egyptian kings boasted of their strong arm, and the arm was a common symbol of power. God breaks Pharaoh's arms and strengthens the arms of Babylon's king, placing his own sword in his hand (30:24-25). In the exodus it was God's outstretched arm that defeated Pharaoh.

insights.title: No medicine
insights.body: Pharaoh's broken arm is not bandaged so it cannot heal (30:21). What happens when a power that others have trusted is permanently weakened?

31.summary: Ezekiel warns Pharaoh by comparing him to Assyria, once a towering cedar envied by all the trees of Eden, which God cut down and sent down to Sheol for its pride.
31.lookfor: Watch how the cedar is described in its glory, why it is cut down, and how the other trees respond in the world below.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: The mountains famed for majestic cedars.

names.name: Eden
names.gloss: The garden of God, pictured here as a forest of great trees.

names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, pictured as beneath the earth.

insights.title: Remember Assyria
insights.body: Assyria had dominated the Near East for two centuries, yet Nineveh fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC, only about twenty-five years before this oracle. Ezekiel asks Pharaoh, "Whom are you like in your greatness?" (31:2). If mighty Assyria could fall, so could Egypt.

insights.title: The Assyrian or a cypress?
insights.body: Verse 3 reads "the Assyrian was a cedar in Lebanon" (31:3). Some scholars suggest a slight change to the Hebrew giving a cypress, a cedar in Lebanon, making the whole poem about Pharaoh. Most translations keep the traditional reading, which fits the warning from history.

insights.title: The world tree
insights.body: A cosmic tree reaching to the heavens, watered by the deep and sheltering every creature (31:4-6), was a widespread ancient image of a great empire. Daniel describes Nebuchadnezzar's kingdom as a tree that is cut down in the same way. Jesus' parable of the mustard seed turns the image upside down.

insights.title: The trees of Eden
insights.body: All the trees in the garden of God envied this cedar (31:9). Ezekiel links Eden with the great powers, as with the king of Tyre in chapter 28. Pride in God-given greatness is the failure of the first humans repeated at the scale of empires.

insights.title: Sheol
insights.body: Sheol (31:15-17) is the usual Hebrew name for the place of the dead, where all go down, great and small. The Old Testament says little about it in detail. The pit and the lower parts of the earth are parallel expressions in this chapter.

insights.title: So that no tree exalts itself
insights.body: The cedar's fall is meant as a lesson "to the end that none of all the trees by the waters exalt themselves" (31:14). Every nation is mortal. The chapter ends bluntly: "This is Pharaoh and all his multitude" (31:18).

insights.title: Mourning for the proud
insights.body: Even creation mourns the fallen cedar (31:15). Why might the fall of a great power cause grief as well as relief?

32.summary: Ezekiel laments Pharaoh as a sea monster dragged out and left for the birds, then follows Egypt down to Sheol, where it joins Assyria, Elam, Edom and other once-terrifying nations lying among the uncircumcised slain.
32.lookfor: Notice the cosmic darkness of verses 7 and 8, then the roll call of nations in the underworld and the repeated phrase about terror in the land of the living.

names.name: Asshur
names.gloss: Assyria, the empire that fell in 612 BC.

names.name: Elam
names.gloss: An ancient kingdom east of Babylonia, in south-western Iran.

names.name: Meshech
names.gloss: A people of central Asia Minor, often paired with Tubal.

names.name: Tubal
names.gloss: A people of eastern Asia Minor, known for metalwork and warfare.

names.name: Sidonians
names.gloss: People of the Phoenician city of Sidon.

names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The realm of the dead.

insights.title: After the fall
insights.body: Both oracles are dated in the twelfth year (32:1, 32:17), about 585 BC, after Jerusalem had fallen. Egypt had failed Judah and still stood. These laments insist it too would go down.

insights.title: Monster in the net
insights.body: Pharaoh thinks he is a young lion but is really a monster thrashing in the waters (32:2), and God hauls him out in a net (32:3). The image echoes old poems of God subduing the sea monster. Ezekiel uses it to show that no earthly power is beyond God's reach.

insights.title: Sun, moon and stars darkened
insights.body: God will cover the heavens and darken sun, moon and stars (32:7-8), recalling the plague of darkness over Egypt. The prophets use cosmic darkening for the fall of empires, and Jesus uses the same language in speaking of the end.

insights.title: Swords under their heads
insights.body: Honoured warriors were buried with their weapons, their swords laid under their heads (32:27). Archaeologists have found such warrior burials in the ancient Near East. The nations in this chapter, by contrast, lie among the uncircumcised and slain, an image of shame without honourable burial.

insights.title: Terror in the land of the living
insights.body: Again and again the dead nations are described as those "who caused terror in the land of the living" (32:23-32). Assyria, Elam, Meshech and Tubal were famed for brutality. The violence they spread defines them even in death.

insights.title: A tour of the underworld
insights.body: Like Isaiah's taunt over the king of Babylon, this chapter pictures the dead greeting a fallen king in Sheol. It is not a detailed teaching on the afterlife but a poetic way of saying that every empire ends in the same grave. The oracles against the nations close here.

insights.title: Pharaoh comforted
insights.body: Pharaoh will see the other fallen nations "and will be comforted" (32:31). What kind of comfort is it to find that others share your fate?

33.summary: Ezekiel is recommissioned as Israel's watchman and calls the despairing exiles to turn and live; then a refugee arrives with news that Jerusalem has fallen, Ezekiel's mouth is opened, and he rebukes both the survivors in Judah and the exiles who enjoy his preaching without obeying it.
33.lookfor: Compare the watchman passage with chapter 3, notice the exiles' question in verse 10, and watch for the moment the long-awaited news arrives.

insights.title: The book's turning point
insights.body: The watchman charge (33:1-9) repeats Ezekiel's commission from chapter 3, marking a new beginning. Until now his message was mostly judgment; from here it becomes mostly hope. The hinge is the arrival of the refugee in verse 21.

insights.title: How then can we live?
insights.body: The exiles say, "Our transgressions and our sins are on us, and we pine away in them. How then can we live?" (33:10). For the first time they accept their guilt, but it has turned into despair. God answers with an oath that he has no pleasure in the death of the wicked (33:11).

insights.title: The city has been defeated
insights.body: The refugee arrives in the tenth month of the twelfth year (33:21), roughly January 585 BC, about five months after Jerusalem fell. Ezra's later journey from Babylon took about four months. A few manuscripts read the eleventh year instead.

insights.title: The mouth opened
insights.body: The evening before the refugee came, God opened Ezekiel's mouth, and he "was no longer mute" (33:22). This fulfils what God had said at his call and on the day his wife died. The years of restricted speech are over.

insights.title: Abraham was one
insights.body: The survivors among Judah's ruins argue, "Abraham was one, and he inherited the land; but we are many" (33:24). They treat the promise to Abraham as a guarantee of ownership. Isaiah makes a similar appeal to Abraham to comfort the faithful, but Ezekiel says these claimants live in bloodshed and idolatry (33:25-26).

insights.title: A lovely song
insights.body: Ezekiel has become popular: people say, "Come and hear what the word is" (33:30). But to them he is "a very lovely song" (33:32), a performer with a pleasant voice. The Hebrew for song here often means a love song or entertainment. James warns against hearing the word without doing it.

insights.title: Hearing without doing
insights.body: "They hear your words, but they don't do them" (33:32). What makes it possible to admire a message, even enjoy it, without letting it change anything?

34.summary: God condemns Israel's rulers as shepherds who fed themselves while the flock was scattered, promises to search for and shepherd his sheep himself, to judge between the sheep, and to set over them one shepherd, his servant David, in a covenant of peace.
34.lookfor: List what the shepherds failed to do, then compare it with what God says he will do, and notice who God sets over the flock at the end.

names.name: David
names.gloss: Israel's great king; here a future ruler from his line, since David himself had died four centuries earlier.

insights.title: Kings as shepherds
insights.body: Across the ancient Near East, kings called themselves shepherds of their people; Hammurabi of Babylon did so in his law code. In Israel the image was rooted in David, the shepherd boy made king. Ezekiel's shepherds (34:2) are Judah's kings and rulers.

insights.title: The weak, the sick, the lost
insights.body: The shepherds have not strengthened the diseased, healed the sick, bound up the broken, brought back the strays or sought the lost (34:4). God promises to do every one of these things himself (34:16). The list reads like a job description the rulers ignored.

insights.title: I myself will be the shepherd
insights.body: "I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep" (34:15). Psalm 23 already called Yahweh my shepherd. Jesus' parable of the lost sheep and his claim to be the good shepherd draw directly on this chapter, as does his compassion on crowds like sheep without a shepherd.

insights.title: Sheep and goats
insights.body: God will judge "between sheep and sheep, the rams and the male goats" (34:17), because the strong sheep foul the water and push the weak aside (34:18-21). Jesus' picture of the Son of Man separating sheep from goats echoes this scene. The flock itself is accountable for how it treats its weakest members.

insights.title: My servant David
insights.body: God will set up "one shepherd over them... even my servant David" (34:23). David had been dead for about four hundred years, so this is a coming king from his line. Jeremiah promises the same, Jewish tradition reads it as the Messiah, and Christians see it fulfilled in Jesus, the son of David.

insights.title: A covenant of peace
insights.body: The covenant of peace (34:25) uses shalom, meaning wholeness and well-being, not just the absence of war. It includes safety from wild animals, rain in its season and fruitful land (34:25-27). Isaiah uses the same phrase for a covenant that will not be removed.

insights.title: Leaders who feed themselves
insights.body: "Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves!" (34:2). How might this chapter speak to anyone who holds responsibility for others, in church, family or public life?

35.summary: Before the mountains of Israel are promised restoration, Mount Seir, the land of Edom, is condemned to perpetual desolation for its ancient hatred of Israel and its plan to seize the land after Jerusalem's fall.
35.lookfor: Notice the repeated because and therefore, what Edom said about the two countries, and how the punishment mirrors the crime.

names.name: Seir
names.gloss: The mountain country of Edom, south-east of the Dead Sea.

names.name: Edom
names.gloss: Descendants of Esau, Israel's brother nation and long-time rival.

insights.title: Why Edom again?
insights.body: Edom was already condemned in chapter 25. It reappears here because chapter 35 sets Mount Seir against the mountains of Israel in chapter 36: one will be desolate, the other flourish. Edom stands for every enemy that tried to profit from Israel's fall.

insights.title: Perpetual hostility
insights.body: Edom's "perpetual hostility" (35:5) uses a Hebrew phrase for an age-long enmity, going back to Jacob and Esau in the womb. Amos also condemns Edom for pursuing his brother with the sword. God answers with a perpetual desolation (35:9).

insights.title: Two nations will be mine
insights.body: Edom said, "These two nations and these two countries will be mine" (35:10), meaning the territories of Israel and Judah, "whereas Yahweh was there" (35:10). The land was empty of people but not of its God. Edom forgot whose land it was.

insights.title: Edom moves west
insights.body: After Jerusalem fell, Edomites moved into southern Judah, as Arab tribes, including the Nabataeans, pressed into Edom's own homeland. The region around Hebron came to be called Idumea, and King Herod the Great was of Idumean descent.

insights.title: Blood will pursue you
insights.body: "Since you have not hated blood, therefore blood will pursue you" (35:6). Edom handed over Israelites to the sword in their calamity (35:5). Obadiah describes Edomites standing at the crossroads to cut off fugitives.

insights.title: Judgment that mirrors the crime
insights.body: "As you rejoiced over the inheritance of the house of Israel because it was desolate, so will I do to you" (35:15). Edom's punishment matches its own conduct point for point. The prophets often present judgment as people reaping what they sowed.

insights.title: Words God hears
insights.body: God says he has "heard all your insults" (35:12) and "I have heard it" (35:13). What does it mean that God takes note of what is said about his people in their worst moments?

36.summary: God speaks comfort to the mountains of Israel, promising they will be farmed and peopled again, and announces that for the sake of his holy name he will gather Israel, cleanse them, give them a new heart and his own Spirit, and make the land like Eden.
36.lookfor: Notice the reasons God gives for acting, the sequence of gather, cleanse, new heart and Spirit in verses 24 to 28, and what the nations will say at the end.

names.name: Edom
names.gloss: Israel's neighbour, singled out as having claimed the land.

insights.title: Mountains blessed
insights.body: In chapter 6 Ezekiel prophesied against the mountains of Israel; now he speaks to them with hope: "I am for you" (36:9). They will shoot out branches and bear fruit for a people about to return (36:8). The same land that bore judgment will bear blessing.

insights.title: For my holy name
insights.body: Israel's exile made the nations say, "These are Yahweh's people, and have left his land" (36:20), as if he had been unable to protect them. God says, "I don't do this for your sake, house of Israel, but for my holy name" (36:22). Restoration rests on God's own character, not on Israel's merit.

insights.title: Sprinkled with clean water
insights.body: "I will sprinkle clean water on you" (36:25) uses the language of priestly purification. Water mixed with the ashes of a red heifer was sprinkled to cleanse those defiled by contact with death. Israel needs to be cleansed from the impurity of idols.

insights.title: A new heart and spirit
insights.body: "I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you" (36:26). Jeremiah promises a new covenant written on the heart, and Hebrews quotes it. Many link Jesus' words to Nicodemus about being born of water and Spirit to this passage, which a teacher of Israel would have known.

insights.title: My Spirit within you
insights.body: "I will put my Spirit within you" (36:27). The Hebrew ruach means spirit, wind and breath, a wordplay Ezekiel exploits in the next chapter. Christians read the promise as fulfilled when the Spirit was poured out at Pentecost.

insights.title: Like the garden of Eden
insights.body: Passers-by will say, "This land that was desolate has become like the garden of Eden" (36:35). Isaiah uses the same image for Zion's restoration. The renewal of people and land go together.

insights.title: Now God will be asked
insights.body: Twice before, God refused to be inquired of by the elders (14:3, 20:3). Now he says, "For this... will I be inquired of by the house of Israel" (36:37). Prayer is reopened as part of the restoration.

insights.title: Shame after grace
insights.body: The people will loathe themselves for their ways after God has restored them, not before (36:31-32). Why might grace, rather than punishment, bring the deepest sense of shame and change?

37.summary: In a vision Ezekiel prophesies over a valley of dry bones, which come together and live when the breath enters them; then he joins two sticks to show that Judah and Israel will be one nation under one king, with God's sanctuary among them forever.
37.lookfor: Watch the two stages of the bones coming to life, the play on breath, wind and Spirit, and the details written on the two sticks.

names.name: Joseph
names.gloss: Here the northern tribes, led by Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh.

names.name: Ephraim
names.gloss: The leading tribe of the northern kingdom, often a name for that kingdom.

insights.title: Our hope is lost
insights.body: The bones are "the whole house of Israel," who say, "Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost" (37:11). The vision answers the exiles' despair after Jerusalem's fall. A nation that seemed dead beyond recovery will live again.

insights.title: Breath, wind, Spirit
insights.body: One Hebrew word, ruach, runs through the passage as breath (37:5), wind (37:9) and Spirit (37:14). The bodies are complete but lifeless until the breath enters (37:8-10), recalling God breathing life into the first human. The point is that only God's Spirit gives life.

insights.title: You know
insights.body: Asked, "Son of man, can these bones live?" Ezekiel answers, "Lord Yahweh, you know" (37:3). It is neither a yes nor a no, but a handing back of the question to the one who can answer it. The bones are "very dry" (37:2), long dead.

insights.title: A pointer to resurrection
insights.body: In context the vision is about national restoration (37:12-14). Yet the image of graves opening became important for belief in bodily resurrection, which Daniel states explicitly. The Talmud records a debate over whether the dead in Ezekiel's vision literally rose, and Jewish tradition reads this passage on the Sabbath during Passover.

insights.title: Unburied bones
insights.body: To lie unburied, scattered on a battlefield, was the worst fate in the ancient world, and contact with bones made a priest unclean. Ezekiel, a priest, walks among them (37:2). The valley pictures defeat, defilement and finality, all reversed.

insights.title: Two sticks, one nation
insights.body: Ezekiel writes Judah on one stick and Joseph, or Ephraim, on another and holds them as one (37:16-17). Israel had been split into two kingdoms since Solomon's death, and the north had been in exile since 722 BC. God promises reunion under one king, as Hosea had.

insights.title: My tent with them
insights.body: "My tent also will be with them" (37:27) uses a word for dwelling linked with the tabernacle. John says the Word became flesh and lived, literally pitched his tent, among us. Revelation's vision of God dwelling with his people echoes this promise.

insights.title: Can these bones live?
insights.body: What in your life, church or world seems as dry as these bones, and what would it mean to answer God's question as Ezekiel did?

38.summary: In the latter days, Gog of the land of Magog leads a vast coalition from the far north against a restored, unsuspecting Israel, and God meets him with earthquake, confusion, plague and fire from heaven.
38.lookfor: Notice who is in Gog's alliance and where they come from, the condition of Israel when he attacks, and who is really directing events.

names.name: Gog
names.gloss: A mysterious ruler from the far north; possibly named after Gyges, a famous king of Lydia.

names.name: Magog
names.gloss: Gog's homeland, listed in Genesis among the descendants of Japheth; its location is unknown.

names.name: Rosh
names.gloss: Either a place name or the Hebrew word for chief, so that Gog is chief prince of Meshech and Tubal.

names.name: Meshech
names.gloss: A people of central Asia Minor.

names.name: Tubal
names.gloss: A people of eastern Asia Minor.

names.name: Gomer
names.gloss: Probably the Cimmerians, nomadic raiders from north of the Black Sea.

names.name: Togarmah
names.gloss: A people in the far north, probably in the region of Armenia.

names.name: Sheba
names.gloss: A trading kingdom of south-west Arabia.

insights.title: After the restoration
insights.body: Gog comes "in the latter years" (38:8) against a land restored and living securely in unwalled villages (38:11). The promises of chapters 34 to 37 have been fulfilled, yet one last threat arises. These chapters answer the question of whether a restored Israel could be destroyed again.

insights.title: Enemies from the edges of the map
insights.body: Gog's allies come from every edge of the known world: Meshech, Tubal, Gomer and Togarmah in the far north, Persia in the east, Cush and Put in the south (38:5-6). Many of the names appear in the table of nations in Genesis 10. The picture is of all the world's hostile powers combined.

insights.title: Rosh, Russia and Moscow
insights.body: Some popular prophecy teachers have linked Rosh with Russia and Meshech with Moscow. Scholars widely reject this, since the names are unrelated in origin, and many translations render the phrase as chief prince of Meshech and Tubal. Gog himself may be named after Gyges, a seventh-century king of Lydia.

insights.title: Hooks in the jaws
insights.body: Gog thinks he is devising his own evil plan (38:10), but God says, "I will turn you around, and put hooks into your jaws" (38:4). God brings Gog against his land "that the nations may know me" (38:16). The enemy is a puppet in a drama God directs.

insights.title: Spoken of in old time
insights.body: God asks if Gog is the one he spoke about through earlier prophets (38:17). Jeremiah and others had warned of a foe from the north. Ezekiel gathers those warnings into a final, climactic enemy.

insights.title: Fire and sulfur
insights.body: God's weapons are earthquake, panic in which every man turns his sword on his brother, plague, hail, fire and sulfur (38:19-22). These recall the plagues of Egypt, the destruction of Sodom, and battles where Israel's enemies destroyed one another.

insights.title: Gog and Magog in Revelation
insights.body: Revelation takes up Gog and Magog as the nations from the four corners of the earth gathered for a final battle after the thousand years, consumed by fire from heaven. Interpretations of both passages vary widely, from symbolic readings to specific end-time timelines. In Ezekiel the stress is on God's final victory and the vindication of his name (38:23).

39.summary: God defeats Gog on the mountains of Israel; his weapons fuel Israel's fires for seven years, his army is buried for seven months to cleanse the land, the birds are summoned to a sacrificial feast, and God promises never again to hide his face from Israel.
39.lookfor: Notice the repeated sevens, the care taken to cleanse the land, the strange feast in verses 17 to 20, and the summary of the whole book's story in verses 21 to 29.

names.name: Gog
names.gloss: The ruler from the far north who leads the final attack on Israel.

names.name: Magog
names.gloss: Gog's homeland in the far north.

names.name: Hamon Gog
names.gloss: The valley where Gog's army is buried; the name means the multitude of Gog.

names.name: Hamonah
names.gloss: A city named in memory of the burial; the name means multitude.

names.name: Bashan
names.gloss: A rich region east of the Sea of Galilee, famous for its fattened livestock.

insights.title: Seven years of firewood
insights.body: Israel will burn Gog's weapons as fuel for seven years (39:9-10), with no need to cut wood from the forests. The number seven signals completeness. Weapons of war are turned to domestic use, an image related to Isaiah's swords beaten into ploughshares.

insights.title: Cleansing the land
insights.body: Burying the dead takes seven months, and teams search the land for any remaining bone, marking it for the buriers (39:12-15). In priestly law a human bone made anyone who touched it unclean. Ezekiel's priestly concern is that the restored land be entirely pure.

insights.title: Hamon Gog
insights.body: The burial valley is named Hamon Gog, the multitude of Gog, and a nearby city Hamonah (39:11, 39:16). Hamon, multitude, is the same word used for Egypt's proud multitude in earlier chapters. The army's great size becomes its epitaph.

insights.title: The great supper of God
insights.body: God invites birds and animals to a sacrificial feast where they will eat the flesh of the mighty (39:17-20). The picture inverts a sacrifice: here the enemies are the victims and the scavengers the guests. Revelation draws on this passage for the angel's call to the great supper of God.

insights.title: Why the exile happened
insights.body: God explains that the nations will know Israel went into captivity because of its iniquity and because he hid his face, not because he was weak (39:23-24). This sums up the book's argument from chapter 1 onwards. The disaster was judgment, not defeat.

insights.title: Spirit poured out
insights.body: The chapter ends, "I won't hide my face from them any more; for I have poured out my Spirit on the house of Israel" (39:29). Joel uses the same language of pouring out the Spirit, and Peter quotes Joel at Pentecost. Gog's defeat leads straight into the vision of the new temple.

insights.title: A face no longer hidden
insights.body: The book's story moves from God's glory leaving the temple to a promise that he will no longer hide his face. What would it mean for a people to live under God's face turned toward them?

40.summary: Fourteen years after Jerusalem's fall, Ezekiel is taken in a vision to a very high mountain in Israel, where a man of bronze with a measuring reed leads him through the gates and courts of a new temple, measuring as he goes.
40.lookfor: Notice the date, what Ezekiel is told to do with what he sees, how many steps lead up to each court, and who is allowed to serve at the altar.

names.name: Zadok
names.gloss: The priest who served David and was made chief priest by Solomon; his descendants led the Jerusalem priesthood.

names.name: Levi
names.gloss: The priestly tribe, from which all priests and temple assistants came.

skim.advice: Most of the chapter is architectural measurement of gates, chambers and courts; skim the numbers, but read the opening commission closely and notice the rising steps and the tables for sacrifice.

insights.title: The twenty-fifth year
insights.body: The vision comes in 573 BC, the twenty-fifth year of exile and fourteen years after the city fell (40:1). "The beginning of the year" translates rosh hashanah, the only time the phrase appears in the Bible. Many note that twenty-five is half of fifty, the Jubilee year when land returned to its owners.

insights.title: A very high mountain
insights.body: Ezekiel is set on "a very high mountain" (40:2), though Jerusalem's temple mount is not especially high. Isaiah and Micah foresee the mountain of Yahweh's house raised above all others. The vision is idealised geography: God's dwelling at the summit of the world.

insights.title: The measuring reed
insights.body: A man like bronze holds a linen cord and a measuring reed (40:3). Zechariah sees a man with a measuring line for Jerusalem, and in Revelation John is told to measure God's temple, and an angel measures the new Jerusalem with a golden reed. Measuring marks something as claimed and protected by God.

insights.title: Six-chambered gates
insights.body: Each gateway has three guardrooms on each side (40:10). Archaeologists have found gates with exactly this six-chamber plan at Megiddo, Hazor and Gezer, often dated to the time of Solomon. Ezekiel's temple gates look like the fortified city gates of Israel's past.

insights.title: Climbing toward holiness
insights.body: Seven steps lead up to the outer gates (40:22, 40:26) and eight to the inner gates (40:31, 40:34). The temple rises in levels as one approaches the most holy place. Space itself is arranged to show degrees of holiness.

insights.title: The long cubit
insights.body: The measuring reed is six cubits, each "a cubit and a hand width" (40:5), the older long or royal cubit of about 52 centimetres rather than the common cubit of about 45. Ezekiel's measurements follow a standard that recalls Solomon's temple.

insights.title: Sons of Zadok
insights.body: Only the sons of Zadok may come near to Yahweh at the altar (40:46). Zadok had served David and was made sole high priest by Solomon. Centuries later the Qumran community, which produced the Dead Sea Scrolls, called its priestly leaders the sons of Zadok.

insights.title: See, hear, set your heart
insights.body: Ezekiel is told to see with his eyes, hear with his ears, and set his heart on all he is shown (40:4). Why might careful attention to detail be a form of worship?

41.summary: The guide measures the temple building itself, its nave and most holy place, its three storeys of side rooms and a large building to the west, and Ezekiel sees walls carved with cherubim and palm trees and a wooden altar-table before Yahweh.
41.lookfor: Notice who enters the most holy place and who does not, the carvings on the walls, and the one piece of furniture described.

skim.advice: Verses 5 to 17 are detailed measurements of walls, side rooms and buildings; skim them, but read verses 1 to 4 on the most holy place and verses 18 to 22 on the carvings and the table.

insights.title: He went in alone
insights.body: The guide goes inward to measure the most holy place (41:3-4), but Ezekiel, though a priest, does not follow. Only the high priest could enter it, once a year. The guide simply announces, "This is the most holy place" (41:4).

insights.title: Solomon's proportions
insights.body: The most holy place is twenty by twenty cubits (41:4) and the nave forty by twenty (41:2), exactly the dimensions of Solomon's temple. The side rooms in three storeys also follow Solomon's plan. The new temple is continuous with the old, yet purified.

insights.title: Cherubim and palm trees
insights.body: The walls are carved with cherubim and palm trees, each cherub with a human face and a lion's face (41:18-19). Solomon's temple was carved with cherubim, palms and open flowers. Palms and cherubim evoke the garden of Eden, guarded by cherubim.

insights.title: The table before Yahweh
insights.body: The only furnishing described is a wooden altar, which the guide calls "the table that is before Yahweh" (41:22). It probably corresponds to the table for the bread of the presence or the incense altar. The word table suggests fellowship as well as offering.

insights.title: No ark
insights.body: The vision never mentions the ark of the covenant, the lampstand or the cherubim over the ark. The ark was probably lost when Babylon destroyed the temple. Jeremiah had said a day would come when no one would miss the ark, because Jerusalem itself would be God's throne.

insights.title: Building as theology
insights.body: Ezekiel's temple has never been built, and the plan was not followed by those who rebuilt the temple after the exile. Jewish tradition has often read it as the pattern of a future third temple. Many Christians read it as a symbolic picture of God dwelling with his people, fulfilled in Christ and the church.

insights.title: The value of details
insights.body: Chapters like this one are often skipped. What might it say about God that the Bible records the plan of a holy place down to the thickness of its walls?

42.summary: Ezekiel is shown the priests' rooms where the most holy offerings are eaten and holy garments kept, and then the guide measures the whole temple compound as a great square wall separating the holy from the common.
42.lookfor: Notice what the priests' rooms are for, why the priests change clothes, and the purpose of the outer wall stated in the last verse.

skim.advice: Verses 1 to 12 describe the layout of the priests' rooms in detail and can be skimmed; read verses 13 and 14 on their use and verses 15 to 20 on the outer wall.

insights.title: Eating the most holy things
insights.body: Parts of the grain, sin and guilt offerings were eaten by priests as their share, and had to be eaten in a holy place (42:13). The law already required this. Ezekiel's temple provides rooms built for it.

insights.title: Holy clothes stay inside
insights.body: Priests must leave their ministering garments in these rooms before going out to the people (42:14). Holiness was thought of as something that could pass by contact, so holy garments were not to touch ordinary life. The theme is repeated later.

insights.title: Holy and common
insights.body: The wall exists "to make a separation between that which was holy and that which was common" (42:20). The distinction between holy and common is a key to the whole vision. Its absence was one of the charges against Jerusalem's priests.

insights.title: A perfect square
insights.body: The compound measures five hundred on each side (42:16-20), a perfect square, just as the inner court and most holy place are squares. The Hebrew text says reeds, which would be enormous, while the ancient Greek translation reads cubits; many scholars prefer cubits. Revelation's new Jerusalem is also perfectly square.

insights.title: Guarding the holy
insights.body: The old temple had been surrounded by the royal palace and defiled by idols (8:5-16). The new design builds protection into the architecture, with walls, gates and courts that keep the holy from being treated as ordinary.

insights.title: Holiness at the centre
insights.body: Ezekiel's plan arranges space in rings of increasing holiness: the land, the outer court, the inner court, the temple and the most holy place. The tabernacle in the wilderness followed a similar pattern. The arrangement teaches that God's presence is both near and set apart.

insights.title: Walls that protect
insights.body: The wall protects the holy from the common. In what ways do people need boundaries to keep what is holy from becoming ordinary?

43.summary: Yahweh's glory returns from the east and fills the new temple, God declares it the place of his throne forever, and Ezekiel receives the measurements of the great altar and the rites for consecrating it.
43.lookfor: Compare the glory's return with its departure in chapters 10 and 11, notice what God says must never happen again in verses 7 to 9, and follow the seven days of the altar's cleansing.

names.name: Chebar
names.gloss: The river in Babylonia where Ezekiel first saw the glory.

names.name: Zadok
names.gloss: The ancestor of the priestly family chosen to serve at the altar.

insights.title: The glory comes back
insights.body: The glory that left by the east gate (10:19, 11:23) now returns "from the way of the east" (43:2) and fills the house (43:5). Ezekiel explicitly links this vision with his earlier ones (43:3). The book's great movement, the departure and return of God's presence, is complete.

insights.title: The sound of many waters
insights.body: God's voice is "like the sound of many waters" (43:2), as was the sound of the creatures' wings in chapter 1. Revelation describes the risen Christ's voice in the same words.

insights.title: Threshold by threshold
insights.body: God complains that the kings set their threshold by his and their doorpost beside his, with only a wall between (43:8). Solomon's palace and temple stood side by side in one royal complex. The dead bodies of their kings (43:7, 43:9) may refer to royal burials or memorial monuments near the temple; interpreters differ.

insights.title: Mountain of God, hearth of God
insights.body: The top level of the altar is called harel, which can mean mountain of God, and its hearth ariel (43:15-16). Isaiah uses Ariel as a name for Jerusalem. The altar is built in stepped levels, like a small sacred mountain.

insights.title: Steps to the altar
insights.body: This altar has steps facing east (43:17), though Exodus forbade steps up to an altar so that a priest's nakedness would not be exposed. Ezekiel's priests are to wear linen undergarments, as later priestly law required. Laws like this are part of why ancient rabbis debated how Ezekiel fit with the law of Moses.

insights.title: Seven days of consecration
insights.body: The altar is purified with blood for seven days, and on the eighth day regular offerings begin (43:25-27). Aaron's priests and the first altar were consecrated over seven days in the same way. The last words are "Then I will accept you" (43:27).

insights.title: The law of the house
insights.body: "This is the law of the house" (43:12): the whole mountaintop is most holy. In earlier law, only the inner sanctuary was most holy. Ezekiel's vision expands the holy zone to the entire summit.

insights.title: Shame before the plan
insights.body: God tells Ezekiel to show the temple to Israel "that they may be ashamed of their iniquities" (43:10). How can seeing something beautiful and holy make people aware of what they have lost or spoiled?

44.summary: The east gate is shut because Yahweh has entered by it, foreigners are barred from the sanctuary, the Levites who served idols are demoted to temple service, and the faithful sons of Zadok receive detailed rules for their ministry.
44.lookfor: Notice why the gate stays shut, who is allowed to sit there, the contrast between the Levites and the sons of Zadok, and what the priests are to teach.

names.name: Levites
names.gloss: Members of the tribe of Levi; here those who had served at idolatrous shrines and are restricted to lesser duties.

names.name: Zadok
names.gloss: The ancestor of the priestly family that stayed faithful.

insights.title: The shut gate
insights.body: The east gate is shut "for Yahweh, the God of Israel, has entered in by it" (44:2). The east gate of Jerusalem's old city, often called the Golden Gate, was sealed centuries ago and remains closed. Early church writers such as Ambrose and Jerome read the shut gate as a picture of Mary's perpetual virginity, a reading kept in Catholic and Orthodox tradition but not generally by Protestants.

insights.title: The prince at the gate
insights.body: Only the prince may sit in the gateway to eat bread before Yahweh (44:3), entering from the inside. He has a place of honour but is not a priest. Ezekiel keeps the ruler close to the sanctuary without letting him control it, as kings had done.

insights.title: Levites demoted
insights.body: The Levites who served at idolatrous shrines will bear their iniquity and only do temple service, slaughtering for the people and keeping the gates (44:10-14). This probably reflects the priests of the high places that Josiah brought to Jerusalem but did not let serve at the altar. Only the sons of Zadok may offer the fat and blood (44:15).

insights.title: Foreigners in the sanctuary
insights.body: Israel had brought "foreigners, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh" (44:7) into the sanctuary to do its work. Temple servants of foreign origin are known from Joshua's day to Ezra's. The phrase uncircumcised in heart echoes Deuteronomy and Jeremiah; the issue is lack of covenant loyalty.

insights.title: Linen, not wool
insights.body: Priests must wear linen, "anything that makes them sweat" being forbidden (44:17-18). Sweat suggests toil and bodily effort, unfit for the holy place. Some rules here differ from Leviticus, such as allowing priests to marry a priest's widow (44:22).

insights.title: Hananiah's three hundred jars
insights.body: The Talmud says that some rabbis wanted to withdraw Ezekiel from use because its laws seemed to contradict the Torah. Hananiah son of Hezekiah is said to have shut himself away with three hundred jars of lamp oil until he had reconciled them. Differences like those in this chapter are what troubled them.

insights.title: I am their inheritance
insights.body: "I am their inheritance... I am their possession" (44:28). Priests received no tribal land; they lived from the offerings and from God himself. The same promise was made to Aaron, and the psalmists use it of every believer.

insights.title: Teachers of holiness
insights.body: The priests "shall teach my people the difference between the holy and the common" (44:23). This reverses the charge in chapter 22 that priests had made no distinction. Restored worship depends on restored teaching.

45.summary: A holy portion of land is set apart for the sanctuary, priests, Levites, city and prince; the princes are commanded to stop oppressing the people and keep honest weights; and the prince is to provide the offerings for the great feasts.
45.lookfor: Notice why the prince is given his own land, the call for honest measures, and which festivals appear in the calendar and which do not.

skim.advice: Verses 1 to 7 and 10 to 15 are land measurements, units and offering quotas; skim them, but read the commands to the princes and the festival calendar.

insights.title: No more oppression
insights.body: The prince gets his own land so that "My princes shall no more oppress my people" (45:8). Samuel had warned that kings would take people's fields, and Ahab killed Naboth to seize his vineyard. Ezekiel removes the motive by guaranteeing the ruler's estate.

insights.title: Just balances
insights.body: "You shall have just balances, a just ephah, and a just bath" (45:10). False weights cheated the poor in the market, and the law and the prophets condemn them repeatedly. In Ezekiel's vision economic honesty is part of temple worship.

insights.title: A sixty-shekel mina
insights.body: Twenty plus twenty-five plus fifteen shekels makes a mina of sixty (45:12). Older Israelite practice seems to have reckoned fifty shekels to the mina, while the Babylonian system used sixty. The odd way of adding it up may combine weights in use at the time.

insights.title: A holy offering of land
insights.body: The holy portion is called a terumah, an offering lifted out for God (45:1), the same word used for priestly contributions. The land itself makes an offering. The Hebrew gives no unit for the measurements; translations supply reeds or cubits.

insights.title: The prince provides
insights.body: All the people give to the prince, and he supplies the offerings for feasts, new moons and Sabbaths (45:16-17). The ruler is the patron of worship, not a priest. David and Solomon provided offerings in a similar way.

insights.title: A different calendar
insights.body: The calendar has purifications in the first month, Passover, and the feast of the seventh month (45:18-25). It does not mention the Day of Atonement or the Feast of Weeks, and the purification rites differ from Leviticus 16. This is another difference the ancient rabbis had to explain.

insights.title: Enough, princes
insights.body: "Let it suffice you, princes of Israel: remove violence and plunder, and execute justice and righteousness" (45:9). Why does a vision about a holy temple stop to address economic justice?

46.summary: Rules for worship in the new temple set out when the inner east gate is opened, how the prince and people enter and leave, the daily, Sabbath and new moon offerings, limits on the prince's gifts of land, and the kitchens where sacrifices are cooked.
46.lookfor: Notice how worshippers move through the gates, the prince's place among the people, and the protections for the people's land.

skim.advice: Verses 4 to 7 and 11 to 15 list offering quantities; skim them, but read the rules for movement through the gates and the laws on the prince's land.

insights.title: No turning back
insights.body: Worshippers who come in by the north gate must leave by the south, and the reverse (46:9). No one goes out the way he came in. Practically it keeps crowds flowing; many have also seen in it a picture of worship that sends people forward changed.

insights.title: The prince among the people
insights.body: The prince goes in with the people and goes out with them (46:10). He worships at the threshold of the inner gate but does not enter (46:2). The ruler is one worshipper among many.

insights.title: Morning by morning
insights.body: A lamb is to be offered every morning (46:13-15). The law of Moses commanded a lamb each morning and evening, and in the late monarchy there was a morning burnt offering and an evening grain offering. Ezekiel's vision mentions only the morning.

insights.title: The year of liberty
insights.body: If the prince gives land to a servant, it returns to the prince in "the year of liberty" (46:17), the Jubilee. Land given to his sons stays with them. The aim is that no one's inheritance is permanently lost (46:18).

insights.title: Protecting family land
insights.body: "The prince shall not take of the people's inheritance, to thrust them out of their possession" (46:18). Prophets before Ezekiel had condemned those who added house to house and field to field. Land in Israel was held in trust from God, not traded freely.

insights.title: Temple kitchens
insights.body: The chapter ends with kitchens: one for priests to cook the most holy offerings, and four in the corners of the outer court for boiling the people's sacrifices (46:19-24). Peace offerings were shared meals eaten before God. Worship included feasting together.

insights.title: Worship in motion
insights.body: The temple's rules choreograph how people move. What do the ways we arrange worship teach about God and about ourselves?

47.summary: A stream flows from under the temple threshold and grows into a great river that turns the Dead Sea fresh and lines its banks with ever-fruitful trees; then God sets the borders of the land and gives resident foreigners an inheritance alongside Israel.
47.lookfor: Measure the river's depth with Ezekiel, notice what happens to the sea and what does not change, and watch who receives land in the closing verses.

names.name: Arabah
names.gloss: The rift valley of the Jordan and the Dead Sea.

names.name: En Gedi
names.gloss: An oasis with springs on the western shore of the Dead Sea.

names.name: En Eglaim
names.gloss: An unknown spring, probably near the northern end of the Dead Sea.

names.name: Hamath
names.gloss: A city in Syria marking the traditional northern limit of Israel's land.

names.name: Hauran
names.gloss: A region east of the Sea of Galilee, south of Damascus.

names.name: Tamar
names.gloss: A place south of the Dead Sea marking the southern border.

names.name: Meriboth Kadesh
names.gloss: Kadesh, the desert oasis where Israel camped and Moses struck the rock.

skim.advice: Verses 13 to 20 list the borders of the land; skim the place names, but read the river vision closely and the closing verses on foreigners.

insights.title: Ankle, knee, waist, swimming
insights.body: The man measures the stream every thousand cubits: ankle-deep, knee-deep, waist-deep, then a river too deep to cross (47:3-5). No tributary is mentioned; it grows on its own. The life that flows from God's presence increases the further it goes.

insights.title: The Dead Sea healed
insights.body: The sea (47:8) is the Dead Sea, so salty that nothing lives in it. Ezekiel sees fishermen spreading nets along its shores from En Gedi to En Eglaim (47:10). The image is of the most lifeless place on earth teeming with life.

insights.title: Salt marshes kept
insights.body: The swamps and marshes "will not be healed. They will be given up to salt" (47:11). Salt was precious for preserving food and was required with offerings. Even in a renewed world, the vision keeps a place for salt.

insights.title: The river of life
insights.body: Trees on both banks bear fruit every month, with leaves for healing (47:12). Revelation's river of the water of life, with the tree of life bearing fruit every month and leaves for the healing of the nations, draws directly on this. Both recall the river flowing from Eden.

insights.title: Living waters
insights.body: Psalm 46 speaks of a river that makes God's city glad, Zechariah of living waters flowing from Jerusalem, and Joel of a fountain from Yahweh's house. Jesus, at the Feast of Tabernacles, promises rivers of living water flowing from within those who believe.

insights.title: Twelve equal shares
insights.body: The land is divided among the twelve tribes "one as well as another" (47:14), with Joseph receiving two portions for Ephraim and Manasseh (47:13). The borders follow those given in Numbers, west of the Jordan. The promise to the patriarchs is renewed.

insights.title: Inheritance for foreigners
insights.body: Resident foreigners who have children in Israel are to receive an inheritance "as the native-born" (47:22). Earlier law commanded love for the stranger, but did not give them land. Ezekiel's vision goes further than any previous law in including outsiders.

insights.title: Have you seen?
insights.body: The guide asks, "Son of man, have you seen?" (47:6). What would it look like for God's life to flow into the most lifeless places you know?

48.summary: The land is divided into equal strips for the twelve tribes, with a holy portion in the centre for the sanctuary, priests, Levites, city and prince, and the city with twelve gates named after the tribes is given a new name: Yahweh is there.
48.lookfor: Notice the order of the tribes north and south of the holy portion, the placement of the sanctuary and the city, and the city's name in the final verse.

names.name: Hethlon
names.gloss: An unidentified place on the northern border, probably in Lebanon.

names.name: Hamath
names.gloss: A Syrian city marking the northern limit of the land.

names.name: Hazar Enan
names.gloss: A town marking the north-eastern corner of the land.

names.name: Tamar
names.gloss: A place south of the Dead Sea on the southern border.

names.name: Meribath Kadesh
names.gloss: Kadesh, the desert oasis on the southern border.

names.name: Zadok
names.gloss: Ancestor of the faithful priestly family.

skim.advice: Verses 1 to 7 and 23 to 29 list the tribal portions and verses 8 to 22 the holy district; skim the measurements, but notice which tribes sit nearest the centre and read the closing verses about the city.

insights.title: Equal strips
insights.body: Each tribe receives one horizontal strip running from the eastern border to the sea (48:1-7, 48:23-27). Unlike the allotments in Joshua, the shares are equal and arranged by design rather than history. The land is ordered around the sanctuary at its heart.

insights.title: Who sits where
insights.body: Judah and Benjamin, the tribes of the southern kingdom, sit on either side of the holy portion. Dan, Asher, Naphtali and Gad, descended from Jacob's sons by Bilhah and Zilpah, are placed at the far ends. The order seems to reflect both honour and history.

insights.title: Not to be sold
insights.body: The Levites' land must not be sold or exchanged, "for it is holy to Yahweh" (48:14). The whole layout protects holy land from commerce and the people's land from the prince (45:8). Israel's restored life has no room for the land-grabbing that marked its past.

insights.title: City and temple apart
insights.body: The temple stands in the priests' portion, while the city lies in a separate common area to the south (48:10, 48:15). In the old Jerusalem, palace and temple adjoined. Ezekiel's vision separates the seat of worship from the seat of civic life.

insights.title: Twelve gates
insights.body: The city has twelve gates, three on each side, named after the tribes of Israel (48:31-34). Levi, who has no land, has a gate here, and Joseph has a single gate in place of Ephraim and Manasseh. Revelation's new Jerusalem also has twelve gates bearing the names of the twelve tribes.

insights.title: Yahweh is there
insights.body: The city's name will be "Yahweh is there" (48:35), in Hebrew Yahweh shammah. It is the book's last word. The book began with God appearing in exile and his glory leaving Jerusalem; it ends with his presence defining the city.

insights.title: No temple in it
insights.body: Revelation's new Jerusalem has no temple, "for the Lord God, the Almighty, and the Lamb, are its temple," and its gates are never shut. Ezekiel's ordered land with God at its centre is one of the main sources for that final vision of the Bible.

insights.title: Defined by presence
insights.body: The city is known not for its walls, wealth or king, but for the fact that God is there. What would it mean for a community today to be known chiefly by that?

intro.who: Ezekiel son of Buzi, a priest taken to Babylon with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC, speaks in the first person throughout. Jewish and Christian tradition treats the book as his, and most modern scholars agree that its core is his work, though many think his followers arranged and expanded it.
intro.when: Its dated oracles run from 593 BC, five years into the exile, to about 571 BC, so the book spans the years just before and after the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC.
intro.why: It tells exiles why Jerusalem fell, insisting that God's judgment was just and that his glory had left the defiled temple, and then promises a new heart, a revived people and a holy temple with God living among them again.
